Mr. Speaker, I am glad to add my remarks on Bill C-139. First, I would like to comment on the remarks made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bloomfield), who indicated that by debating Bill C-139 and trying to deal with some of the issues and principles involved, we as the Opposition were delaying the issuance of tax refunds to Canadians.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: That is true.
What about the T-4s?

One of the reasons Canadians are having difficulty trusting this Government and politicians today is the kind of comment emanating from Parliamentary Secretaries and Ministers who sit opposite. They try to bluff their way through and create the illusion that they are being responsible by giving us a Bill consisting of 295 pages and containing a number of complex issues. The Government first presented this Bill last December, waiting over a year to introduce it. In the meantime, the Government brought in a number of other bills, including C-131, C-132 and C-133. These Bills reduced Family Allowances, pensions and other matters and will affect a large number of Canadians who are in difficulty because of the economic times which have been created by the Liberal Government. The Government did all of those things and yet tells us that we should not take a careful look at this complex piece of legislation, which probably most Members opposite do not understand if the truth were known.
Tax refunds probably will be delayed this year. The Government needed an excuse. It needs the capital and the money it will save by doing that. Also the computers will be down in the Department of National Revenue which will prevent the refunds from being issued on time. There were ample opportunities for the Government to bring in this Bill so that it could be adequately discussed. For the Government to claim now that we are holding up this legislation is a sham, and it should be ashamed.
1 have three points that I would like to outline. They have been made in a variety of ways by a number of Members. Dealing just with the complexity of this Bill, let me open the Bill at random. At the top left-hand side under Section 54, it reads:
"(5.4) Where there has been a disposition by a non-resident of a life insurance policy in Canada by virtue of subsection 148(2) or any of subparagraphs 148(9)(c)(i) to (ii) and (iv.l), the insurer under the policy shall, for the purposes of subsections (5.2) and (5.3) be deemed to be the taxpayer who acquired the property for an amount equal to the proceeds of disposition as determined under section 148."
1 would challenge one of the Parliamentary Secretaries or the Minister to stand up and interpret that paragraph for us very quickly. It contains four or five references which I pulled out at random. This paragraph identifies one of the major problems we have in Canada with our whole tax system by
showing how very complex it is. It creates great difficulties for the taxpayer.
Mr. Lyman J. Maclnnis, a senior partner of Touche, Ross and Company in Toronto and President of the Chartered Accountants Institute in Ontario, delivered a speech a little while ago in which he made three basic points about the tax system in Canada. He indicated that the tax system in Canada should be self-assessing. In other words, the individual taxpayer is required to respond to this system on his own behalf. The majority of Canadians are required to interpret legislation like this and then establish their tax position. They are required to deal with the Department of National Revenue, which employs a large number of specialists who devote their full time to dealing with tax policy. Mr. Maclnnis also said there should be an ability for self-assessment by having tax measures in clear and unmistakable language. Let me again refer Canadians to the random opening of Bill C-139 that I have just made. Is that an indication of clear, unmistakable language?
The courts have identified this problem. They, too, have said that tax legislation should be in clear, understandable language. There is hardly any argument, whether from an accountant, a lawyer or a Member of Parliament, that this is a basic problem of our tax system. Mr. Maclnnis gives us a number of examples going back to the first tax Bills right up to the most recent. He gives us the impression that the accountants, those dealing with this matter, are not able to respond satisfactorily to the needs of their clients and individual Canadians. The language in our Income Tax Act has created confusion. It is difficult for any of us to deal with it. Unless the language is cleared up and we start to deal with this problem adquately, it will go on resulting in more and more specialized people dealing with measures that are more and more confusing to the average Canadian. We will have a dichotomy, a separation, of interests and understanding. In fact, we are left as a country in confusion over the whole tax system.
I have two other points. One is on behalf of the Canadian people. I will quickly run through proposals that will affect individual Canadians through their personal income tax changes. One is the replacement of the IAAC deduction with the forward averaging measure. Then there are the changes referring to the taxation of employee benefits; the limitation on deduction for investment interest costs; a reduction of federal dividend tax credit to 34 per cent of cash dividends; the repeal of the capital gains revenue deductions; the requirement of professionals to inventory work in progress; the prevention of excess transfer of claims for $1,000 investment and pension income deductions; the restriction of $1,000 pension deduction to retired persons; the restriction of personal exemption for non-resident dependants; and deindexation to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. These are all things that affect individual Canadians through their personal income tax. It gives us a situation whereby Canadians will face higher income taxes as a result of these provisions.
I see that my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker. I could list things that affect business, making it very difficult

February 21, 1983

for business to operate. Included are the capital cost allowance changes and so on. These are leading to a situation where individual Canadians will be less able to look after themselves, where business is less able to function, to grow and create the economic activity which is important to our country. We end up with a government that is increasing activity daily, increasing its spending, its deficits, its borrowing. We have more and more emphasis on Government activity and less and less ability for individuals and business in Canada to carry on with theirs. We are forcing Canadians-this is the crime of which Bills like this are part-to depend upon a state that cannot look after them.
That is the legacy of the Liberal Party. That is the result of years and years of mismanagement. It started off with John Turner and Donald Macdonald, and it is continuing under this regime.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on Bill C-139, it is interesting to point out that the Government has used its right to extend the sitting hours so that we are sitting through the lunch hour to discuss this very important piece of legislation. The Government is once again proving that it will use the mechanisms of the House to try and rush through important legislation.
This bill represents the economic and moral bankruptcy of the Government. As well, it represents its bankruptcy of leadership. We have before us a 300-page piece of legislation which would bring in a number of amendments to the Income Tax Act. Our taxation system is already tremendously complicated. An article written by Robert J. Jackson, the head of the political science department at Carleton University, for yesterday's Toronto Star states in part:
Income tax forms have grown so complicated over the years that great numbers of confused Canadians seek professional help to fill them out. Yet difficulties at the individual level are but pale reflections of the confusion and insecurity that is generated throughout the system by flaws in the taxation process.
Yet that process will be further complicated if the legislation is passed at this time. Another layer of amendments is being added to the Income Tax Act, another layer of confusion which will make it hard for the ordinary Canadian to understand what taxation is all about. The Government should be introducing comprehensive legislation, rewriting the whole Income Tax Act, making income tax something that ordinary Canadians can understand again, doing away with the litany of tax deductions which help those at the top, and doing away with the confusion which it has created when it has introduced as it is now doing, piecemeal changes to the taxation system.
I said earlier that the Government suffers from a lack of leadership. It is evident in every piece of legislation that comes before the House. It is evident in the very acts and speeches of cabinet Ministers of the Liberal Government. They have lost the ability and the will to lead the country. Only the problems of the Conservative Party keep the Liberal Government in power at this time.
Canadians are facing record unemployment. Canadians are suffering because of lack of leadership by the Government.
Income Tax
Canadians want the Government to provide leadership. Canadians want jobs for themselves and for their children. They want the Government to introduce legislation which will help them in each and every part of the land. This Bill does not do that.
The Bill, we are told, must be passed because to delay it would affect the amount of time required by the Government to process 1982 income tax forms and refunds. However, let me remind Your Honour that many of the articles in the 300 pages of the Bill are from a budget which was introduced in the House in November of 1981. The Government did not act at that time. Other parts within the Bill come from the June 28 budget of 1982. Again, the Government did not act to introduce legislation in the House. Other parts of the Bill come from the October, 1982 budget of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Again the Government did not introduce legislation in the House.
The Government had 13 months in which to introduce this legislation but it failed to act. Now we are speaking during the lunch hour as a result of an attempt by the Liberal Government to rush this legislation through, to pass it before Canadians who will be affected have a chance to respond to their Members of Parliament and to the Liberal Government. That is part of the moral bankruptcy of the Government, part of its mechanisms which stifle debate and prevent Canadians from understanding the taxation system in this land. It is part of the mechanisms used by the Liberal Government to prevent Canadians from participating in the democracy of this land, because they are not able to understand what is going on in the House of Commons and are not aware of what is in the legislation being discussed.
This does not apply to all Canadians. Those Canadians who are represented by powerful lobbies, by interest groups which meet with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Cabinet, do have the ability to change legislation. They have the financial resources to ensure that their loopholes are enhanced. They have the ability to ensure that Government introduces legislation which, as this legislation does, removes the percentage of tax to be paid by those who earn the most. Significant deductions will be allowed to those who earn the most. The tax percentage of those people who earn over some $130,000 a year will be dropped from 43 per cent to 34 per cent, a tremendous reduction for those who could best sacrifice.
The Prime Minister has appeared on TV and radio to discuss the necessity of sacrifice and of Canadians co-operating together, yet the Bill states that those who have the most, who earn the most, who are best able to sacrifice, will pay less to the Government of Canada. What kind of justice or taxation system is that? What kind of Government would introduce taxation legislation enabling the rich to become richer at a time when we have unparalleled unemployment across the country? We must oppose the legislation because it is unfair and because it is complicated. Our taxation system should not be so complicated that Canadians cannot fill out their own

taxation forms. However, we oppose it mostly because it represents the bankruptcy of the Government, the fact that the Government is now moving from legislation to legislation, from speech to speech, from PR effort to PR effort, without any concrete plans which would help the average Canadian.
This approach by the Government, by the PR team headed by the Liberal Senator Keith Davey, whose sole job, financed by the taxpayers of Canada, is to keep the Liberal Government going, represents the moral decay of the Government. It represents the Government's loss of concern over the fate of the average Canadian. It represents the fact that the Government has only one purpose, and that is to retain power. Canadians deserve better than that, and I hope all Hon. Members will oppose this legislation and force the Government to introduce comprehensive tax legislation and economic policies so that Canadians can once again trust the leadership of their Government.

Mr. Speaker, most people today have been speaking about measures included in Bill C-139 and how they will affect Canadian taxpayers. However, I would like to talk about a measure that should have been included in any Bill amending the Income Tax Act but is not in Bill C-139.
When the previous Minister of Finance introduced his ill-fated budget of November, 1981, he promised reform of the Income Tax Act that would promote equity and fairness. Bill C-139 stems from that budget, yet it does very little to promote the goal of equity and fairness.
As a good example of this, I would like to discuss Section 31 of the Income Tax Act which deals with the deductibility of farm losses. Under the Income Tax Act, there are three classes of farmers. There are those whose major source of income is farming but who may earn some other income not related to farming; there are those whose chief source of income is not farming, or a combination of farming and some other source of income, but who still carry on farming with a reasonable expectation of a profit; and third, there is the taxpayer whose chief source of income is not farming but who carries on farming activity with no reasonable expectation of making a profit. This category is commonly referred to as the "hobby farmer."
My concern is with the second class of farmer and how Section 31 applies to this taxpayer. Under Section 31, the second class of taxpaying farmer, whose major source of income does not come from farming but who can reasonably be expected to make a profit from his farming, can only deduct farming losses of $5,000 a year. This $5,000 deduction has remained constant since it was introduced in 1952, over 30 years ago. Not once has it been increased to reflect general inflation or specific cost increases to agriculture. If this deduction had been indexed since 1952, I suggest it would today be worth $20,000, a four-fold increase. In other words, the deduction is only worth one-quarter of its 1952 value. This is obviously inequitable and unfair to this class of farmer.
It is fairly easy to speak of Section 31 in the impersonal terms of a Government tax accountant, but what we often fail to see is the terrible impact that such a measure can have on an individual or a family. In my riding, I have had a number of individuals who are trying to start up a farming operation come to see me because Section 31 of the Income Tax Act is effectively wiping them out.
I would like to discuss one particular case because I think it illustrates the problem very well, and it was brought to my attention just last summer The farmer in question was born and raised on his parents' ranch, and he inherited one-quarter of it in 1970 upon the death of his father. Being raised on the ranch and trained as a rancher, he knew the business and felt he could make a living and support a family. During the two years that the estate was being settled, my constituent worked hard with an exploration company and saved every cent he could to develop his share of the ranch. When it was finally his in 1972, he began fencing in the land to raise livestock. He acquired some cattle and purchased necessary farming equipment, paid for by taking out a bank loan and by working parttime off the farm.
In 1975, he applied to the Farm Credit Corporation for a loan to buy additional equipment, put up a barn, purchase a mobile home, instal power and do some necessary roadbuilding. He was turned down for a Farm Credit Corporation loan.
In spite of this setback, my constituent continued to work his land, and in addition he began to consolidate his property which had been in nine separate parcels. He also sold low, wet land where half of his hay crop had been flooded out and purchased upland hay land. However, in spite of his efforts my constituent had to begin full-time work off his farm in 1977 to get sufficient money to continue developing the farm. Basically, this was because the Farm Credit Corporation had been unwilling to give him the loan necessary to develop the land. From 1977 to 1981, my constituent worked at a sawmill located in a remote area of B.C. accessible only by aircraft and he put every penny he could into his farming operation. During this interval he could only farm approximately 84 days a year, weekends and holidays, because of his outside job. In June of 1981 he again applied to the Farm Credit Corporation for a loan, this time being successful, and he began to farm full-time once again.
Since 1978 he has cleared over 200 acres of hay land and more than doubled the amount of hay produced. He started to build a home on his land, but at this time he, his wife and their three young children live in the basement of this partially completed dwelling, without the benefit of running water. His land is good and he is finally on the brink of reaping the benefits of the 10 years of hard labour that I have just described.
However, last spring Revenue Canada struck, in the form of tax auditors. Because of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act, my constituent can claim only $5,000 a year in farming losses for the 1977 to 1981 period, even though he plowed all the money
February 21, 1983

he earned into his farm during that period. His actual losses during this time ranged annually from $7,500 to almost $17,000 and totalled over $48,000. Under Section 31, however, he could deduct only $20,000 in total, leaving him with losses disallowed for this period of over $28,000. The back taxes and penalties now assessed are impossible for him to pay unless he sells land, which at this time is very difficult.
Now, if the $5,000 limit established in 1952 had been indexed, this rancher would have been well within his allowable deductions and would perhaps be facing a profitable future. Instead he faces potential bankruptcy at the hands of his Government. And what will be gained? A family on Unemployment Insurance, if not welfare, defaulted loans, and the lost production of a new farm. Where is the equity and fairness in this?
My constituent, his accountant and myself have tried to reason with Revenue Canada, to no avail. The Act appears to be written in stone. When I wrote to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) about this case, I received a one-page, three-paragraph reply. The Minister said in his last paragraph, and I quote:
Yours is one of a number of representations I have received on this issue, and I thank you for bringing to my attention these examples of the impact of present tax law.
What a farce! The Minister made no effort to see that this inequitable piece of legislation was amended. He acknowledges the problem but refuses to take any action whatsoever. And so here we have Bill C-139, legislation which could have amended this injustice and put some incentive into the system but does not.
The Secretary/Manager of the B.C. Cattlemen's Association put the situation into perspective when he wrote to me recently on Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. He said, and I quote:
In my own opinion the problem stems from the lack of clear national policy regarding development of new agricultural production units (farm or ranch) and recognition of such policy through the Income Tax Act. If we as a society want to encourage development of new farms and ranches, we should say so and provide for it through taxation.
Truer words were never spoken. Bill C-139 fails miserably to address this very issue and the silence and inaction of the Minister of Agriculture simply underlines this lack of a clear national policy. But, Mr. Speaker, it is not simply the young farmer starting up a new operation who is being hurt by this counter-productive policy. Professionals who wish to invest in agricultural operations are being actively discouraged from doing so by Section 31.
As an example, the expansion of the Canadian equine industry has been severely curtailed by Section 31. People cannot be persuaded to invest in a horse-breeding operation when they can only deduct $5,000 a year against losses. When we now see outstanding horses selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars, the $5,000 deduction becomes even more ludicrous.
The Canadian Horse Council has recognized this and in a February, 1983 article in "Hoof Beats" the Council made the
Income Tax
reform of Section 31 its first task. In that article they said, and I quote:
The agreed upon first task of the Horse Council will be to see if Section 31 of the Income Tax Act can be either eliminated or at the very least, have the limited loss liability amount raised from its present S5.000, the amount it was first set at when the section was enacted way back in 1951. From becoming an intended incentive to agriculture, it has become a disincentive.
This is plainly the case. The present structure of the Income Tax Act is antiquated. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Agriculture have been negligent in failing to introduce measures in Bill C-139 that would either repeal Section 31 or bring the $5,000 deduction to a more reasonable limit of $20,000 or more.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Their failure to do so has resulted in a great deal of hardship to those attempting to get started in agricultural ventures, thus posing a serious threat to Canadian agriculture. If the Government is truly serious in its oft-stated concern for this sector of the economy, then let it immediately introduce a simple tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised to be here at this time participating in this debate at second reading of this Bill. I thought this was the lunch hour. Apparently under the spirit of parliamentary reform, lunch hour will not be what it used to be. If that spirit carries on, I am afraid that reform will be an improper description of what will be occurring in the future. However, two can play the same game.
The Bill we are debating today is a classic example of the absolutely absurd budgetary system we have in this country. On November 12, 1981, well over a year ago, the then Minister of Finance brought in a budget. We have the absurd situation in this country where at the instant a Minister of Finance tables a notice of Ways and Means, basically a piece of paper which says "I hereby give notice of a Ways and Means Motion", that has the effect of law. From that point on the Government can start collecting the tax. He does not need to make a budget speech before doing that. At any time any Minister can table a piece of paper called a "notice of Ways and Means", and from that point on the tax can be collected. It is absolutely incredible.
That system was put in place at a time when there was some sort of adherence to practices and traditions. Following immediately upon the Ways and Means motion was a budget debate. That was followed immediately by Bills flowing from the budget. The time lapse between that period and it becoming law, having been passed by this House, the other place and approved by the Governor General, was very short. Through sloppiness, contempt of Parliament, incompetence and a

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
variety of other reasons, we have the absurd situation where the rules governing parliamentary democracy have been so distorted that over a year after the budget was brought in we are debating the legislation.
We did not get to see the Bill until a year after the budget was presented. For over a year Canadians were forced to pay the tax. They were forced to adhere to the law. They did not know the law. They still do not know it. They have received T-1 forms which they are required to fill out. They are to send in the money they owe for taxes even though they do not know what the law is. Even though they do not know the law, they have received their T-l forms and are expected to comply. It is incredible.
The sorry situation is that we have become more tolerant of that incredible situation. It is an insult to Parliament and to those Canadians who elected us to carry on with this absurd situation. By comparison, let us look at the situation in the United States.
Prior to the end of January, the executive presents a budget to both Houses of Congress. That budget is then considered for eight months. It is amended and changed by their parliamentarians, the people elected to represent the population. The subsequent legislation is passed before the end of the fiscal year, October 31 of the year. In other words, there are eight months of consideration by their legislators. Frequently, in fact most of the time, there is significant amendment, depending on what the legislators want. The law is then passed and comes into effect. That is the way it should be.
In a democracy, the most important group is the electorate. The second most important group is those elected by the electorate. No one in Government has the right to introduce laws imposing conditions and forcing people to obey something not passed by the legislature. That is what democracy means in that country.
We have the absurd situation of Canadians being expected to comply with the law that Parliamentarians, those whom Canadians elected to represent them, do not even become aware of until nearly a year later. It is an absolutely absurd situation. One of the serious consequences of this is contempt by Canadians for Government, for Parliament and the law. When that contempt extends to the Income Tax Act, we are in serious difficulty.
Many of my colleagues and others have spoken of the excellent address given by the chairman of the Ontario Association of Chartered Accountants dealing with the complexity of the Act and the inability of the average person, and, indeed, those who have been trained such as chartered accountants and lawyers, to comprehend the Income Tax Act. He said it is an absurd situation when we have a self-assessing system. Individuals are expected to know the Act, to comply with it and to voluntarily send in their tax based on the self-assessment system. How can one self-assess, how can one do a proper job of fulfilling that responsibility, if one cannot understand the Act?
I am one of the better educated people in this country. I stayed in school until they would not have me any more. I am not suggesting that I am the brightest, among the brightest, or anything like that. However, after 20 years of publicly-supported education, 1 still cannot understand the Income Tax Act. I humbly suggest that either there is something wrong with the education system or, more likely, something wrong with the system that generates this kind of Income Tax Act.
More important in terms of the attitude of Canadians toward this Act is the increased evidence of tax avoidance. It is not only practised by a few sharp cookies, but practised far and wide. It is estimated that the underground economy, that is, the economy which escapes the taxman and recognition by the information takers in Government, is in the order of $50 billion. That is not the cash economy but the barter economy. The lawyer says to the carpenter that he will draw his will if the carpenter will do some work in his rumpus room. The dentist would say to the plumber, I will look after your children's teeth if you will put the plumbing into my cottage or farm. The house painter says, it will cost you $2,000 for me to paint your house unless you pay me in cash, in which case I will be able to do it for $1,200.
That, Mr. Speaker, is not hypothetical. It is not a rare situation. According to hard evidence gathered by research groups, that sort of thing constitutes something like $50 billion of our economy. It is an underground economy. People simply have so much contempt for this Income Tax Act that they are now using schemes which heretofore were not contemplated. A chartered accountant in Calgary who has been in business 30 years told me that clients are asking him to do things now in terms of avoiding tax which had he suggested to them ten years ago they would have fired him. Ten years ago there was a feeling that one did not avoid tax because that was unpatriotic. It was unfair. Maybe it was not illegal in the strict sense but a good Canadian did not avoid tax. Today people are saying to their accountants or lawyers: "Find me a way to avoid tax because I do not have any respect for a Government which would bring forward tax Acts like this, and I do not intend to pay one penny more than I am absolutely required to do".
That situation, Mr. Speaker, is extremely dangerous for Canada, is extremely dangerous for the future, and leads inevitably to what we are seeing-an increase in the number of tax collectors, an increase in the Gestapo of the National Revenue Department, to go out and force people, and it changes Canada significantly.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow my learned colleague to my left, the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), because, as he says, he is one of the most educated men in this House; but at the same time that is not saying very much.

This is my first opportunity to speak on this piece of legislation, Bill C-139, and the people of Canada have to understand that this is the result of three Liberal budgets-or could we call it two and half Liberal budgets? The first one of November, 1981, was brought in by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), who was then Minister of Finance. Of course, he is no longer Minister of Finance. He was driven from that position by the Liberal caucus members, which caused him to be a fugitive now in the safe bosom of External Affairs. The Cruise missile is as nothing compared to the missiles which that former Minister of Finance got from his colleagues in the Liberal caucus as a result of his attempt to perform the functions of a Liberal Finance Minister.
He was the gentleman, Mr. Speaker, who said in Halifax on September 9, 1980-the former Minister of Finance, and I want to identify him as Mr. MacEachen, the now Deputy Prime Minister-"It was to create jobs, improve living standards and to promote greater equity that I took on the position of Minister of Finance". Of course, it is exactly for those reasons that the poor devil was driven from the post of Minister of Finance. He created to jobs. In fact, we have lost 582,000 jobs since the summer of 1980. He created no jobs. We have the highest unemployment in our history, 1,600,000. Living standards have done nothing but fall since he took the portfolio on in 1980.
He said he wanted to promote greater equity. It was in his budget of November, 1981 that he attempted to provide this equity. And, Mr. Speaker, this became the most elastic budget ever presented in the House of Commons. Its elasticity became 100 per cent. That poor Minister became a whirling dervish, retreating from this proposal of reform, so-called, retreating from that proposal. Within seven days he had twirled and whirled and we had about 18 reverses of the positions he had taken in that budget of November, 1981. And he whirled and twirled until I believe it was June, 1982, when he brought in another budget, and again he was forced to twirl because the budget which he brought in did not provide equity.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, he was given the coup de grace and removed from that position. We now have a new Minister of Finance the former Minister of Energy. A gentleman more widely known outside as Mr. Lalonde. He brought in another document in October of this year.
It is the process of those three budgets which is interesting. In the October document, the new Minister of Finance reserved again many of the provisions which were in the first two budgets of his predecessor. It was funny, Mr. Speaker, and I have remarked on this before, how the Hon. Members of the Liberal backbenches in this House sat there on the night of November 21, or whenever it was, of 1981, when the Minister of Finance of the day said he was going to bring more equity and reform into the system, and applauded all his attempts to reform the system. The same people sat here in October, 1982 applauding the successor to the then Minister of Finance as he reversed all those so-called attempts to reform and to create equity. What was equitable under the MacEachen budget was inequitable under the Lalonde budget. What was fair under
Income Tax
the MacEachen budget was unfair under the Lalonde budget. What was reform under the MacEachen budget was "deform" under the Lalonde budget. And the same people sat there giving the same claps, cheers and smiles as they saw their two Ministers of Finance completely reverse themselves in the period of 15 months.
Well, the result of that abominable procedure is this Bill which is before the House. So that the public might understand, I believe it has 289 pages and it took the Government 389 days. A budget was brought in in November, 1981, yet this Bill was not tabled in this House until December 7, 1982. Some 389 days after the great budget of reform of Mr. MacEachen, we have the Bill finally produced in this House, and there were hundreds of changes in between.
The present Minister of Finance says we are to deal with this budget fairly quickly or else he will not bring in a new budget. I say, Mr. Speaker, thank God for that. The longer we can dwell on this Bill, the better chance we have to stopping the new Minister of Finance from bringing in his new budget; because if his new budget is anything like the budgets we have had since February 18, 1980, it is in the public interest to stop it from being brought into this House. I recommend to the Hon. Members of this House that we talk on this Bill from now until the end of 1983 to prevent another Liberal abomination of a budget coming before this House.
When I came into office in June, 1979, Mr. Speaker, I found left behind the debris from two Liberal budgets. I had to appear in this House and introduce legislation to try to salvage something out of two previous "Chretien" budgets. Oh, we have had Ministers of Finance, Mr. Speaker, from the Liberal Party; we have had Chretien, MacEachen, Lalonde-

Well, I have to refer to the Donald Macdonald budget. He is no longer in the House. He is on to a good thing outside the House now. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to comment briefly on the debate that has consumed much of the Question Period these past few days in the House of Commons. I am referring to the on-going dialogue concerning the umbrella Weapons Testing Agreement which Canada and the United States have recently signed. Unfortunately, in the confusion over just what has and has not been agreed to, we have seen the very heart of the issue recede into the background, overshadowed by the rhetoric and moral posturing of some of the Opposition.
What I think is important for the House of Commons and Canadians to recall is that Canada and Canadians fully support NATO and the Alliance. We believe that a "credible deterrent" is needed to maintain peace with liberty. The two-track approach which we support calls for actively engaging in negotiations that could contribute to meaningful and verifiable arms control and disarmament agreements, while at the same time working with our Allies to modernize our theatre and conventional defence forces in Europe so that they will in fact form a deterrent to the frightening build-up of Soviet armaments.
I am confident that we will give serious consideration to any serious Soviet proposals that would enhance the chances for effective and verifiable agreements, but it is obvious that real progress can only be made on the basis of the principle of mutual security. I would like to remind Members of this House and all Canadians that the crux of the issue at hand is our security, without which we are unlikely to continue to enjoy peace, independence, and hope. We would all be well advised not to lose sight of these facts.

Madam Speaker, today the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women will release a report called "A Working Majority: What Women Must Do For Pay", which documents the deplorable conditions of women in Canada's paid work force.
The pervasive and debilitating ghettoization of women's jobs has intensified, as more than 70 per cent of women are in clerical, service, sales, and processing jobs and one-third are employed in jobs where men earn twice as much. Women are even being displaced by men in the few well-paid job areas such as teaching.
Just as shocking as the lack of opportunities and inadequate pay for women is the finding that the federal Government itself discriminates against women.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, correspondence is on file going back to July 29, 1980, to the former Minister responsible for small craft harbours, requesting that action be taken to improve government facilities in Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, and I made special mention of the need for over-all dredging in the entire harbour.

February 21, 1983
This request was followed up by another letter on September 10, 1981. On October 7, 1981, the then Minister of Public Works informed me that the extensive survey required to determine the dredging quantities involved could not be carried out until late fall, with a final report expected around the middle of February, 1982.
I again wrote to the Ministers of Fisheries and Public Works on February 1, 1982, and again on March 12, 1982, and later on July 26, 1982, to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), since shipping comes under his authority. On October 13, 1982, I wrote to the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) endorsing all previous requests, followed up by another letter on December 7, 1982, and a further letter on February 2, 1983.
On February 9, 1983, the present Minister of Fisheries informed me that the Public Works dredge had arrived in Lunenburg Harbour, but that dredging would only be carried out in the area adjacent to the government wharf. This will be helpful, but it is imperative that the entire ship channel be dredged if the harbour is to function at full capacity and allow ships to make adequate use of the repair facilities and berthing space, without scraping bottom.
In conclusion, I ask the Minister of Fisheries why this necessary task is not to be completed while the equipment is on site.

Madam Speaker, the proposal of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to change the Crowsnest Pass freight rate has not been submitted to Parliament. To date we have a Liberal Party position which is not the law of the land, and may never become so. I do not believe that Liberal Party proposals are entitled to be publicized at public expense. Nevertheless, the federal Department of Agriculture has placed large advertisements in Quebec newspapers favouring Crow change. The full-page ad appearing in today's edition of The Gazette in Montreal is worth $4,535.
These ads are slanted to convince Quebec farmers that a changed Crow rate is good for them. For example, The Gazette ad says that higher transportation costs will prevent Western pork and beef producers from becoming more competitive with their Eastern counterparts. Yet the Transport Minister's Crow statement predicted that this could mean an expansion in the output of the Western livestock industry of about $1 billion by 1990.
The arguments being used to sell the Minister's proposal in the West are being downgraded in the East. This is classic Liberal divide-and-rule politics. If Cabinet Ministers persist in using public money to sell partisan policies, then provision must be made for public funding of opposing viewpoints. This
principle is well established in the equal time provisions for the broadcasting of differing party points of view.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the Statute Law relating to Income Tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to continue my remarks on Bill C-139. Before I was interrupted pursuant to Standing Order 21, I was saying that Bill C-139 was brought in as a result of some three budgets that have been brought down by the Government. They were the budgets of November, 1981 and June, 1982 and the mini-budget of last fall. This legislation, which deals with tax policy, took considerable time, some 15 months, to come to the House. It comprises some 300 pages. It is extremely complex and people do not understand it. It certainly has a detrimental effect on the performance of the Department of National Revenue. The Department has indicated that Canadians will not receive their income tax refund until this legislation is passed.
I was attempting to point out earlier how the Department of National Revenue certainly has no qualms about collecting taxes before appropriate laws are passed. However, we see how the bureaucracy is acting with regard to tax refunds. Unfortunately, this omnibus Bill does not address many problems that people such as my constituents face.
There are many farmers in my constituency as it is a rural, agricultural constituency. Many of the measures in this legislation do not deal in a systematic and helpful way with the problems faced by farmers in my area.
I would like to reiterate one of the matters raised by our agriculture critic earlier in the debate. It concerns the fact that one of the major changes introduced in Bill C-139 eliminates the income tax averaging annuity contract and replaces it with a system of forward averaging. In many respects, this is not the best answer to the problems that some of the farmers or small-businessmen face in our area. Within Bill C-139 we find that there is a reduction in the capital cost allowance in the first year. This is of particular concern in respect of farm equipment which would have been eligible under the previous provisions for a 30 per cent allowance in the first year. Under

the new proposals, only 15 per cent of the capital cost allowance would be eligible. I would point out in this respect that if our agricultural and other primary producers received a proper benefit in income tax on the operating costs of their farms, the rest of the economy would move again.
I notice that you are getting ready to indicate that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I would just mention that we oppose this Bill because it is seriously flawed and because we think it should not be dealt with in its present form at this time.

Member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) had been really concerned about taking part in debate on meaningful issues in the House, he could have put his ten minutes to use and possibly spoken on Bill C-139. We will try to assist him in the future and, hopefully, move him over here to the Opposition where he can ask questions to his content.
We certainly support the Speaker in trying to sort this problem out in the House. We realize the hardship the Hon. Member faces on occasion.
I did not think that 1 would have a chance to speak on this Bill, but the Hon. Member for London-Middlesex (Mr. Bloomfield) made it possible as a result of his attempt at parliamentary reform and kinship across the floor by forcing us to sit through the lunch hour.
As you know, 1 come from a riding in southern Ontario. Many of my constituents are very concerned about Bill C-139. In my riding there are people in the small business field, in the agricultural field and even in the major industrial field, and amongst all of them there is confusion as a result of the complexities of this Bill. There have been some 500 changes to the Income Tax Act in the last 11 years, 42 of them in the Bill before us. People do not know where to turn for understanding. The only people the Bill seems to assist are the accountants, and even they are frustrated.
Having had some military experience and thus something to do with regulations and having spent some eight years in university, I thought I would be able to understand the Bill. However, being a moderate man from a rural riding, I need some assistance, and this Bill does not offer it.
One of the things that concerns people in my riding, for example, is general averaging. It is being replaced by forward averaging and that sounds fine. When we read the definition of "accumulated averaging amount", however, this is what we are faced with in clause 69(8) on p. 162 of the Bill, which reads as follows:
(o) "accumulated averaging amount" of an individual at the end of any taxation year means the product obtained when
(i) the amount, if any, by which the aggregate of
(A)	the individual's accumulated averaging amount at the end of the immediately preceding taxation year, and
(B)	the amount deducted under subsection (1) by the individual in computing his taxable income for the year
exceeds
(C)	the amount added under subsection (2) by the individual in computing his taxable income for the year
is multiplied by
(ii) the ratio, adjusted in such manner as may be prescribed and rounded to the nearest one-thousandth or, where the ratio is equidistant from two one-thousandths, to the greater thereof, that the Consumer Price Index for the 12 month period that ended on the 30th day of September next before that year bears to the Consumer Price Index for the 12 month period that ended immediately before the commencement of that 12 month period; and
The people of Haldimand-Norfolk find that very confusing, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps the Minister and the people in his Department do not. We are just average, rural folk, and we would like the Government to try to make things a little simpler for us. The small business people and the farmers in my riding need help, not more regulations or definitions or restrictions. Small-businessmen are concerned about interest rates and about the decreased purchasing power of the individual. The farmers are not concerned about how much paper work they have to do to calculate their taxes; they are concerned about the cost of equipment, fertilizer, help, fuel and everything they need on the farm. They are concerned about the low return they receive for their work, not how difficult the Government can make the Income Tax Act.
I looked for the capital gains exemption and a new valuation day date which was promised by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the last election campaign. That is what the farmers need; it is what they count on for their retirement plan. They also need something to stimulate their business, not more bankruptcies and foreclosures. How can they be proud of their country when they consider the economic outlook?
Figures issued by the OECD on economic outlook indicate that in the areas of economic growth and productivity, Canada ranks last of the 24 leading industrialized countries. We have the second highest unemployment rate in the industrialized world, second only to the United Kingdom. Japan has an unemployment rate of 2.25 per cent, and Germany 8.25 per cent, 5 points less than ours. Canada is the only OECD country in the top ten, whose industrial productivity has decreased. We rank tenth behind the United States, Japan, Germany, France, United Kingdom, Italy, Belgium, Denmark and Sweden. All other countries registered some increase but Canada experienced a drop of 0.2 per cent.
How can small businessmen and farmers make plans? The figures I have quoted do not demonstrate leadership. They cannot plan five years ahead when the governing Party changes the Act every time it presents a budget. All levels of business are concerned-individuals, small business people, major corporations, farmers, fishermen, even municipal and provincial Governments.
In the pre-budget statement presented to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in January, 1983, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce stated as follows on p. 19:
February 21, 1983

We have expressed our view on previous occasions that the post-budget process is now grossly over-extended. We hope that we will not see again a situation where legislation is passed in 1983 relating to the 1981 taxation year. We believe that the government should adopt an approach where draft legislation is tabled on budget night. We are appreciative of the change in approach taken for Bill C-139 where detailed explanatory notes were released. We believe this approach should be followed in the future, and even be amplified, making it much easier to react to the draft legislation in a timely fashion.
We believe that it is generally agreed that the Income Tax Act has become too complex in the past few years, especially in the areas relating to small business. The reason why this has occurred is not difficult to establish; every budget in the past few years has added another layer of complexity onto those which have gone before, so the whole system is now virtually staggering under its own weight.
When the Chamber of Commerce expresses that view, Mr. Speaker, we are in trouble.
How does all this affect Canadians? There have been four different versions of a budget-the one introduced in November 1981, the version that amended it on December 18, 1981, the one that was dropped on us on June 28, 1982, and then, of course, the one of October 27, 1982. In addition, there have been all sorts of minor announcements and clarifications, such as the January 1982 announcement of employee benefits.
These other things I mentioned concern us and we want to see them clarified and brought into better perspective in the budget. We could talk about this for days and hours, but I am glad to have had the time to raise a few of the issues that are of concern to people in my area and which I think should be of concern to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is totally incomprehensible. I realize that it is not the first one that we could not understand and that nobody else, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) could understand. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) also has problems with it.
1 was glad to see Members of the NDP participate in the debate and slam the Liberals today. I had been worried about their close collaboration with the Liberals when they were saying that they would not campaign against them in the constituencies in the foreseeable future. But they are with us on Bill C-139, Mr. Speaker.
This Bill is partly the result of the worst budget ever brought down. That was in November 1981 when the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was Minister of Finance. He decided to correct everything without giving any real thought to what the effects might be. Consequently, he brought in a horrible budget to close the so-called loopholes. Actually, they were tax incentives that had kept such industries going as the building industry. Suddenly the door was slammed. I shall not soon forget the look of absolute horror on the face of the Deputy Prime Minister who was then the Minister of Finance. It was pointed out to him by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) that the immediate result of his budget at that time was to put some 20,000 construction workers out of work in the Province of British Columbia. Until that time I believe he had gone through it as a kind of exercise in some sort of paper war so that he would look good to people who were fretting about tax loopholes in the construction industry. Possibly this was his first realization that he had actually put a lot of people out of work, simply because of what he thought was a good speech
Income Tax
given in support of a budget that some people believe to this day he had not read before presenting.
All the changes in the budget ever since then have been piecemeal and have frequently left the impression that they have postponed the implementation of various sections, have cut amounts in half, have cut percentages in half or by a third, or found some other amelioration for the rather savage changes. They did not withdraw the entire budget, and they withdrew very few major portions of it.
I would like to speak for a few minutes about the problems with the terminology in the Bill and in taxation matters in general. I have received many letters about the inability of people to understand the taxation rules until too late. One such letter was from a lady in my riding. I wrote to the Minister about it. I would like to refer to parts of this letter and, rather than identifying the woman who wrote it, I will call her Ms. X. The second paragraph indicates that at present she is age 99 and is fortunate enough to have a gentleman, whose address is such and such, to look after her affairs and have power of attorney. This gentleman was most upset because he had paid her taxes for 1981 on time but on a once-a-year basis. He did that because her total income in 1981 was $16,843. More than $14,000 of this income came to her only in November or later in 1981. This would likely be because of savings bonds or Government bonds. She received her income in November but was expected to pay taxes in June, on the first instalment for the year. She did not understand that and made only a onetime payment for 1981.
I run into quite a few people in my riding whose incomes come from sharecropping arrangements which they have back on family farms in Alberta or Saskatchewan. This is a payment they receive whenever the Government makes a wheat payment. It is not necessarily phased out once every quarter of the year; quite often it comes in in the fall.
I wrote a letter to the then Minister of National Revenue in which I said that it was difficult to understand why the Government wished to have my constituent pay through three-quarters of the year on income she would not receive until the fourth quarter of the year. It is no wonder that the gentleman who was looking after her affairs was puzzled. In part my letter read:
I wonder if you would be kind enough to have your officials look into this matter and determine if proper warning was given to Mr. . . . that Mary ... (aged 99) would be required to pay taxes quarterly apparently based on her total annual income.
I look forward to your early, favourable reply.
I received the usual answer acknowledging receipt of my letter, and then I received a further reply a month after I had written. That was pretty quick time for that group.
As an aside, 1 would like to congratulate the current Minister of Finance. I guess he needs every kind word he can get after the shambles he has made this week and last week of the

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
conduct guidelines of the current Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). But he did something of interest, because I am now receiving letters from the Minister of Finance in answer to ones which I wrote to the former Minister of Finance, the present Deputy Prime Minister, over a year ago. 1 thank him for his letter of January 1982. At least the current Minister is beginning to get the mail answered. Apparently he has something over a year's backlog left to him by the rather feckless Deputy Prime Minister when he was Minister of Finance.
A month after 1 had written asking about this particular lady who paid her taxes on an annual basis until this year, 1 received a reply from the Minister. The first thing she recalled about it all was that not only was she to pay on a quarterly basis, but she owed them so much for the first quarter and so much in interest on the payment she had not made. The answer, which was supposed to please them, was contained in a letter addressed to me from the then Minister of National Revenue, which read in part as follows:
I am writing in reply to your letter of July 14 ... in regard to the income tax affairs of Ms.-
It is true that the requirement to pay tax on income in the year received creates situations where a portion of the tax is required to be paid prior to receipt of the actual income. Self-employed businessmen in summer seasonal operations face a similar problem.
I am sure that would be of great interest to this 99 year old lady! It continued:
In their case, they would not normally be in receipt of any income until the month of July but, nevertheless, would have been obliged to make a quarterly payment of tax in the immediately preceding June and March quarters.
My Head Office officials have reviewed Ms. ... records and have informed me that she was advised during the 1980 calendar year that she may be subject to the instalment requirements.
Now, listen to this; it goes on:
The advice Ms. . . . would have received was in the form of a T7B, Instalment Guide for Individuals, along with a T3T01 remittance form. In addition, Ms. . . . was also charged instalment interest on the 1980 tax assessment.
I trust the foregoing explanation will assist you in replying to your constituent in a satisfactory manner.
Flow on earth do we reply in a satisfactory manner to a 99-year old constituent when the officials claim that because they sent the Instalment Guide for Individuals in an envelope to her in 1980, she should have known that it changed her system of paying taxes, and therefore they will penalize her for not paying them under this system right from scratch. Ridiculous.
I am one-and I suppose the same is true of most Members of the House-who has my income tax forms completed by an accountant. It has gone beyond the scope of most of us to fill out our own income tax forms. I believe Department officials should begin considering the fact that all the accounting could be done by the Department or something, because I do not know how to figure it out. When one tries to read the form which Ms. X was supposed to have understood, one would not believe it. It is ten pages long. It is full of anomalies. It talks about Option A and Option B. I can hardly believe that the poor soul was supposed to understand. In part it read:
General Requirements
If you have a taxable income, you are required to make quarterly instalment payments of income tax unless:
(a)	taxes deducted at source from at least three-quarters of your "Net
Income";
(b)	your chief source of income is farming or fishing; or
(c)	either your Federal Income Tax for 1981 or your estimate of Federal
Income Tax for 1982 does not exceed $400.
Instalment payments of Canada Pension Plan contributions may also be required (see page 7).
There are ten pages in this document, and by the time one gets to page 7 it tells one the following:
Calculation of Canada Pension Plan Contributions.
I am not sure what that has to do with it. Also it indicates:
Estimated Canada Pension Plan Contributions Payable by Instalments.
Perhaps they made a mistake and it should have been page
8.	Who knows? This is the kind of problem with which Members of Parliament are faced because of these omnibus or enormous Bills that contain totally non-understandable English.
How would Hon. Members like to be faced with understanding Clause 12.(1) at page 44, which reads:
Paragraph 20(l)(r) of the said Act is amended by striking out the word "or" at the end of subparagraph (ii) thereof, by adding the word "or" at the end of subparagraph (iii) thereof and by adding thereto, immediately after subparagraph (iii) thereof, the following subparagraph:
"(iv) borrowed money used to acquire an interest in an annuity contract to
which section 12.2 applies, or would apply if the contract had a third
anniversary in the year-
Is that clear? In conclusion I would like to refer to an Act which was passed by the United Nations. We should send down Bills to them. This one was written in simple English, and we are able to understand it very easily. I am sorry I do not have any time left in which to quote from it.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with every other speaker whom I have heard comment on Bill C-139. It is the most complex piece of legislation which this House has seen for some time. Certainly the most complex that I have ever had to deal with since coming here three years ago. The Bill itself, which is to amend the Income Tax Act, is about 300 pages thick.
It is sick.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
It is sick. That is probably right. But it took the Department of Finance another 200 pages in explanatory notes in an attempt to set out to Canadians and to Members of this House what the amendments are all about. It has not been particularly easy for Members of Parliament, for the public and even those who are experts and professionals in the field, to understand what the Government is trying to do here. In fact, one writer, Robert J. Jackson, head of the Political Science Department at Carleton University, in attempting to define what the Government was trying to do, wrote:
In the tax field the two MacEachen budgets, of November, 1981 and June, 1982, were catastrophes that never became law. Neither did Lalonde's minibudget of last fall, which tried to undo the worst damage of his predecessor.
February 21, 1983

What we are attempting to do is to deal with bad amendments which were supposed to have been made less so by a new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
In going over the Bill itself and looking through the explanatory notes it would seem that the present Minister of Finance has resorted to the same kind of twisting and bandying about of an income tax system that in general is totally inequitable. It is particularly inequitable in regard to people at the low end of the income scale. He had an opportunity, I think, in finally bringing this particular Bill before the House, to have made some amendments to the Income Tax Act for which many groups across the country have been calling for quite a number of years. For instance, he could have taken into consideration the findings of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped which travelled across the country listening to disabled groups and individuals about their financial needs and what the Government could do to make life a little bit better for them to help them participate in the mainstream of Canadian life as able bodied individuals have been permitted and allowed to do over the years. There was one simple amendment the Minister could have brought in, to which he said earlier he would give consideration, namely to bring in some amendments to the Income Tax Act which would have offset the cost of disability. A disabled or handicapped person has living costs which are in excess of what an able bodied person has. Very often a person, particularly one with mobility problems, requires special forms of transportation. This is an additional cost to that individual. It should be remembered that most disabled people receive far below what we would normally consider to be an average income. In fact, most individuals have incomes which would be considered at or below the poverty level. The Government could have acted on some of the recommendations made by that Special Committee. Amendments could have been made to the Income Tax Act.
In response to a constituent's complaint in this area, the Minister of Finance stated that his Department was reviewing income tax concessions currently available to the disabled as well as recommendations which were made to our Committee. The Minister of Finance certainly could have made some move in that area without its having a drastic effect on the existing revenue the Government receives.
In another area the Minister could have done something for the disabled people and their families by taking into consideration the financial needs of those who have mobility problems, those who are not sighted and those with other disabilities. Concessions could have been made through the income tax system to allow either the disabled persons or their families to make renovations to their own homes or apartments so as to make them easily accessible for disabled people.
Under current legislation there are many contradictions which make accessibility difficult to achieve. For example, special devices to assist disabled persons in making their toilet should be made tax deductible. What about renovations to make the doorway to the bathroom wider so that the disabled person can have access to the bathroom? The committee felt that in specific instances such as those, the Department of Finance could act immediately to provide deductions without
Income Tax
waiting for presentations from other Departments. That would have been a rather simple thing for the Minister to do had he so chosen. But, he did not.
What about amendments to the Income Tax Act to encourage on-the-job-training for disabled people? The Minister's Department did bring forward an employment program several years ago. It provided some assistance with equipment to allow a disabled individual to fit into the normal workplace. That particular program, to my knowledge, has not been very successful, primarily because the federal Government has not shown an example by bringing in, within its own Departments, adequate training programs or affirmative action programs for disabled people. In the federal Government's own employment practices it still has a long way to go to accomplish some level of satisfaction in that area. The private sector is not likely to act until the Government-and the Committee argued this very strongly-takes a leadership role in employing disabled and handicapped people. From my own experience, especially in small business, small businesses are more open to the suggestion of hiring disabled people than are large corporations and governments.
The Government could have assisted small businesses which recognize that disabled people should be judged for their ability rather than their disability. The very least the Gover-ment could have done was to accommodate the good citizenship shown by the small business community and to assist small businesses to do their job even better.
1 see that my time has run out, Mr. Speaker. I could speak for another 40 minutes on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. It is probably one of the most important events that has ensued with respect to matters incredibly complex. I have heard the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) speak about complexity. He put it within one term of reference. I have a personal term of reference within which I would like to put the complexity. It came about as a result of being aware that I would be speaking today concerning the provisions of the Income Tax Act. I met three tax accountants from a large Canadian Firm in Toronto last Friday. They outlined two points to me. The first one dealt with ordinary accountants, those in small firms in towns like Cambridge. In some cases because of the complexity of this Bill it was beyond their capabilities to understand it fully. The result was that accountants were coming to these large firms to seek advice, but even these large firms found it difficult to give advice in some circumstances.
This tax partner, who deals with international finance and large multinational corporations, made a second point. These particular areas are complex by their very nature, with international implications. However, when compared with the provisions with which a small business person and an accountant advising the small businessman must deal, they bear no

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
absolute relation in terms of their complexity. He asked me if I would point out in my speech the provisions of Section 125(3) of the Income Tax Act and he asked me to defy anyone, through Your Honour-and I see that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) is here-to say exactly what the provisions of Section 125, 1 through 6, mean. I read it over the weekend. I was once a practising lawyer and dealt with a great deal of tax litigation. I will say to Your Honour that ordinary people certainly cannot understand it and accountants do not even have the time to try to understand it. Some do not have the aptitude to do so. The large firms are having a great deal of difficulty, especially with the one section that I pointed out. Taxes are the price that we pay for civilization, and it is a very dear price that we are paying these days.
I would like to discuss three or four aspects of the new provisions of the Income Tax Act. One of the most important, from my perspective because I am a small business critic, concerns RRSPs. Everyone knows that interest expense on contribution to RRSPs made after November 12, 1981, will not be deductible. The provision with respect to deductibility was a tax preference because it was given on the social understanding that it was wise for people to provide for their own retirement. That was a laudable social and public goal. It has been absolutely stripped by the provisions of this particular piece of legislation. The objective of the RRSP, as I say, is to allow savings for retirement. If an individual continually borrows year after year in order to make RRSP contributions, never paying off any of these loans, then the objective of saving for retirement is completely frustrated. However, most lenders require that the RRSP loans be paid off within one year. If one goes to the lending institutions, whether it be the credit unions or the banks, and looks at the advertisements, one finds that they will lend money for the purposes of buying an RRSP, but one of the provisions is that it be paid off within one calendar year.
This is obviously another Government grab for revenue. It is as simple as that. The reality is that if people cannot borrow for the purposes of providing for their own retirement, they will not become involved in RRSPs, which I believe to be a public and social necessity because it deals with the philosophy to which I subscribe, that is, self responsibility. I find the situation with respect to RRSPs nothing short of appalling.
Let me deal with capital cost allowance. Here we are, at this particular point in our history, in the depths of a very deep recession. We are in a situation where the Government will be taking $3 billion out of the private sector and putting it into the public sector. I find this to be absolutely against the grain so far as I am concerned. It is certainly nothing in which I have ever believed, especially at this point in time. There has been an abridgement by the Government. Specifically, I point out Class 29 write-offs, depreciable property.
Your Honour may recall the budget of May 8, 1973, I believe, brought in by John Turner. In his speech on the budget, with respect to Class 29, he said he wanted to create
employment because that was the most imperative social issue at that time. He brought in what is known as the speedy writeoff for manufacturing. In other words, in the first and second years a person could write off 50 per cent of any manufactured machinery purchased. He was holding out a carrot. The former Minister of Finance gave three reasons at that point in time. First, he said it would create employment. I agree, it did create employment. Second, he said it would enhance cash flow. Because that carrot was being held out, the third provision was that we would avoid obsolescence. As I say, to take such a tremendous amount of money out of the private sector and put it into the public sector at this time is totally without foundation or justification.
The third matter I would like to discuss is the corporate distribution tax. I can certainly understand why the Government is proposing it, because it is trying to ensure that salaries are treated in the same manner as dividends. That is where I disagree. I will give a very short example. Under the old system, if a company was taxable at $100, the corporate tax, the small business rate, would be approximately $25, with $75 left over. If a dividend was paid on the $75 under the 1982 scenario, it would amount to approximately $18.75, which was one-quarter of the amount. The total tax involved would be $18.75 plus the $25, so that at the most the taxpayer would be paying $43.75. Under the 1983 budget provisions, with that same $100, there is a quarter off, which makes it $75; there is the corporate distribution or Part II tax, payable by the company, which brings it down to $66.67; and the personal tax on the dividend at one-quarter of the rate, and what we get, really, is $50. The point I am making is that it becomes a question of preference. I understand, because it has been clearly stated, why the Government did this. I have always believed, and still do, that being able to take money out by way of dividends in this-no doubt about it-preferred way, was socially and publicly good. I do not see why it was changed.
I would like to touch briefly on two other areas. One concerns work in progress. I was happy to see that the provisions of the November 1981 budget were changed with respect to professionals such as lawyers and accountants who could not be incorporated. What irritated me is that it discriminated against architects and engineers. I do not think there are any Members in the House who have not received letters from their local engineers about these discriminatory provisions. In my view, the reason these professional people were discriminated against was that it was said they could incorporate and were therefore eligible for the small business rate of tax. However, from everything that I have been able to ascertain, if I could use a word of the street, the architects and engineers are really getting "shafted" with respect to this provision, whereas there are proper remedies with respect to lawyers and accountants.
I had hoped to make a couple of points more, but I see that Your Honour is giving me the nod to signal that my allotted time has expired.
February 21, 1983
