speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-139, to amend the Statute Law relative to Income Tax (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak to Bill C-139 which deals with the amendments to the Income Tax Act. This Bill is the most complex Bill since 1971, and it is some 297 pages long. Moreover, it has taken the Government 398 days to bring this Bill into the House.
As a new member, elected in October, 1 must say that it is very hard for me to be able to absorb 298 pages in such a short period of time, the changes from the budgets of November, 1981, June 28, 1982 and October 27, 1982, and 350 changes to the Income Tax Act.
Today I want to speak on a few of those. My riding, which is Timiskaming, stretches from Lake Nipissing through to James Bay. My constituents have a concern with some of Bill C-139, and I would like to take a few moments to describe some of the proposed changes we would like to see. The proposed taxation on professional work in progress has been withdrawn for professions outlined under Section 125(b)(f) of the Income Tax Act: medical doctors, lawyers, accountants, dentists, veterinarians and chiropractors. The measures, however, remain the same for architects and other professions.
The one profession I would like to mention to you today is that of insurance adjusters. I have a constituent who has a very small operation and is concerned with regard to the taxation on work in progress in the adjuster's office. His understanding
Income Tax
of this reform means that at a certain date it will be necessary for him to calculate the amount of time he has spent on each file. The time will be converted into a financial figure and, once this is done, taxation would apply.
His letter went on to say that if this is to happen as his operation has a very minimum margin of profit it would probably force this individual out of business. This is one concern that we have in this riding in regard to Bill C-139.
Another area which is of grave concern is the taxation of northern benefits. To the north of my riding, which enters into the James Bay area which takes in Moosonee and Moose Factory, at any time it is very hard to get qualified people into the area. Under Bill C-139 the taxing of northern benefits is not only going to jeopardize the individuals who are now in Moosonee and Moose Factory, but in future trying to interest employees whether they be in the Moose Factory hospital or with the James Bay Board of Education or with the Ministry of Natural Resources in that area, is going to be very, very difficult. And I hope that this will be taken into consideration not only for my riding in northern Ontario but in other northern areas across Canada.
I would like to move on to another area in which there is great concern with Bill C-139. Prior to my being elected to the House of Commons I was a salesman, and the taxation of the travelling expenses of individuals who are employed as salesmen is of great concern. There are many salesmen provided with a car by their company, not only in my riding but across Canada, who work for a very low income and work on an incentive basis. An individual might drive anywhere up to 125,000 miles a year, and he is being taxed for possible use of this car during the weekend or in the evening. I must say that it is very wrong to tax an individual who happens to be making in the neighbourhood of $12,000 a year on the one benefit that he might have, a car sitting in his yard for a short period of time over the weekend, and if he uses this car in any sense, whether it is going down the street to shop with his wife or whether it is just going out to a private home, he is being taxed on that.
I must say that at the same time there are companies across Canada today which are saying to their salesmen: "We are no longer going to supply you with a car. You have to go out and buy your own car. Because of this taxation we feel it is much better for you to own a car and then in turn be paid by the company." Once again, if you are in the income range of $12,000 to $16,000, a car payment on top of everything else today-everyone recognizes the problem with the way the economy is, and the fact that selling is not the same as it was five years ago-is another burden. I would like to say once again that that is another concern with Bill C-139.
There is another very, very large concern in I think almost every area across Canada, and that is taxation in regard to MURBS, in regard to apartment buildings that are much needed across this country. In my riding of Timiskaming a new
23056

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
industry was started three years ago, and we had the opportunity of having a contractor come into our area who was willing to build apartment buildings that were required. But under the taxation of the budget of November, 1981, this was taken away from private individuals who wanted the opportunity to invest money in apartment buildings. I urge this Government to reconsider this matter because this provision must be put back in, in order not only for the riding of Timiskaming to have the opportunity for the much needed apartment buildings but because there are numerous towns and cities across this country that require that extra building.
In closing I must say that under Bill C-139 it is very, very important that we look after the small businesses across this country, small businesses which make up this country. With a bill such as this, 296 pages long, and the problems that a small businessman has today in trying to understand a Bill such as this, I, and I think all Members on this side of the House, see the urgency of making this task easier. We have to make it a lot easier for the individuals because, as we all realize in these times, it is very hard to break even, let alone have to worry about hiring a chartered accountant, which some of these small businesses or individuals really cannot afford to do.
In closing I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am very pleased to have had the opportunity to speak on this Bill. My people in the riding of Timiskaming are certainly pleased that you have given me that opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, in order for a taxation system to be successful it has to be intelligible and citizens have to abide by it cheerfully and voluntarily. I think it was the Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) who said it is a price we pay for civilization.
It is becoming increasingly apparent, as the Member who just finished speaking noted, that Canadians are becoming frustrated and bewildered by the complexities of trying to cope with a very complex set of rules and regulations. It is interesting from a historic perspective to recall that when a taxation system becomes too complex and too onerous some irresponsible politicians make great gains by leading so-called tax revolts. I say to the Minister opposite, who I know is a keen student of political history, that Pierre Poujade in France at one time controlled the very balance of power in the French National Assembly by espousing a tax revolution. In the meantime, we have seen a similar phenomenon in the United States, in the State of California, and recently there has been another movement in that regard.
I think that the taxpayers and the business community want more than anything else in this country is some stability and some continuity in the taxing system. It seems to me that the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of National Revenue are inextricably bound together. When one looks at the plethora of Ministers in the last four years and looks at the contradictory policies that have been espoused, it is very easy to see why the business community is in such a quandary about what to do.
Colleagues will remember when the present Minister of Energy (Mr. Chretien) brought in his budget. He never had that budget legitimized. The election came before that could occur. My colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) then became Minister of Finance. That budget was never implemented. Then we had, as many Members have said, that dreadful budget brought in by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) when he was Minister of Finance. We then had the son of that budget, which in some ways was even worse than the first one.
The illegitimate son.

We then have the present Minister of Finance who brought forward a very well accepted economic treatise or statement which really served in the place of another interim budget. Now we are waiting for yet another budget. Just consider that, all within the space of four years.
Looking at the Ministry of National Revenue side, we go back to Tony Abbott in 1979, not so long ago. Well, he is gone. We had the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) in our short-lived administration. We then had the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Romp-key), and now the present incumbent. Again, with all respect, it is difficult to get any continuity or stability with all this turnover of ministers. In fairness, that was not enough time for these gentlemen to have mastered the complexities of the Department and perhaps not enough time for them to have coordinated their particular policies with the Minister of Finance.
However these kinds of fundamental policies as opposed to specific regulations surely need not have suffered as much as they had. I note, not with amusement but with some interest, that in order to make the situation look a little bit better for itself and perhaps more relevant, the Government recently raised the base of the cost of living index. In effect, we are starting off on a much higher plateau for the eighties. This serves to make people forget how badly their standard of living has eroded in the last decade.
Our capital gains evaluation, which was set in 1971, has not been touched. That surely is a great disincentive to the kind of business activity and confidence that the Government should be wanting to instil in ordinary Canadians and the business community. I remember speaking to the then Minister of Finance about this, the present Deputy Prime Minister. I asked him questions shortly after he became Minister. On March 13, 1981 I asked him:
Since it is approximately ten years from valuation day, and since the Minister knows that when assets change hands now they are being taxed heavily on inflation, which I think he would agree is confiscatory, what plans do he and his Cabinet colleagues have to revise or otherwise make more equitable the capital gains tax structure in this country?
The then Finance Minister replied to the effect that he had released a discussion paper on capital gains and talked about
February 21, 1983

the question of indexing. I pursued the matter in a supplementary question to the Minister, asking him about the time frame and about more specific information.
1 quoted a man named Harris who was President of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. He wrote a very good treatise on the ironic situation in which people who benefit from lotteries are not subject to capital gains while people who invest in their country are, and people who save to buy securities from Canadian companies in order to put their children through college or provide for their retirement are taxed heavily in the same way as someone who speculates in or buys foreign securities.
I pointed out to the Minister that there was room here to be more equitable, to tilt toward Canadian securities, to encourage investment in Canadian companies and be fair about the way that capital gains are being assessed. The Minister indicated that he was interested. Accordingly, I wrote him a few days later, and I said among other things:
I am enclosing a copy of Mr. Harris' speech to the Winnipeg Rotary Club as well for your information I am attaching a copy of a letter I sent to Mr. Harris.
I wrote to Mr. Harris bringing to his attention the fact that I had made these representations, based on his speech, in the House of Commons to the Minister of Finance. I suggested that Mr. Harris might wish to take the Minister up on his offer for further information and elucidation about what he said. That was the absolute end of it.
I do not know whether the present Minister of Finance expects to look at changing the capital gains tax. I know there are Members on the other side who share my views. I trust that they will make these kinds of representation because, if the present situation continues and people are taxed on a capital gains for assets based on a 1971 valuation day, they should realize that in many cases their assets are simply confiscated because of inflation and they are punished for having been prudent investors.
There is another point I would like to make in the realm of general policy. That is the need to co-ordinate some of the efforts of the Minister of National Revenue with his Cabinet colleagues. Time and again I have been struck by the anomaly of someone trying to build up a family farm as a part-time farmer to the point where he or she can leave their present employment and become a full-time farmer, but then being frustrated by the rather harsh tactics of the field workers of National Revenue. On an arbitrary basis they disallow a lot of the farmers' deductions, and go back several years to do it.
On the other hand we have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who is constantly espousing the welfare, as is his job, of the farm community in this country. He is making available money through the Farm Credit Corporation and encouraging in every way he can the welfare of farmers. While he is doing this, his Cabinet colleague is chopping down the efforts of those who are trying to achieve the status of full-time farmer. Those kinds of things are very anomalous.
Although it is slightly off the subject, let me point out that it would help to staunch the drain on our taxation revenues if we tied work-training programs to unemployment insurance payments so that people who are in this enforced period of
Income Tax
idleness could at least benefit to some extent from the sustenance that they are getting in order to keep them in a decent position until work is available. It would help them to become more flexible and qualified. I do not see any real effort being made to do this.
There is also the question of the attitude of the Department of National Revenue. I want to pay tribute to the present Minister and his predecessor, the Hon. Member for Grand Fall-White Bay-Labrador, for being very open and available to me and listening to the suggestions I put forward. However, there are many instances, some in my own Province, where a Draconian approach has been taken by field workers and some of the officials. In that regard, and on a bi-partisan basis, I want to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) who, on March 26 of last year, moved the following motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of the Department of National Revenue assuming responsibility for the expenses incurred by a taxapayer whom the Department causes to be investigated, when such investigation by the Department's officials does not result in a suit or claim.
This is sometimes done in quasi-criminal and even criminal cases when an accused is acquitted.
Has my time elapsed, Mr. Speaker? Thank you, Sir.

Mr. Speaker, I enter into this debate this afternoon with some misgivings, given the very serious economic plights of this country and the absolute and inappropriate actions of the Government of Canada. In talking at second reading of this income tax Bill, the basic statutory vehicle through which Government economic policy is implemented, we are in very serious difficulty with the directions of this Government and the principle it is developing. In indicating the direction taken in this particular legislation, the Income Tax Act, and the provisions within it, based on previous budgets by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), the Government missed completely the needs of the consumers in Canada. The individual Canadian is faced with problems of trying to maintain a home or a small business and living in this very negative environment.
There are five criteria, Mr. Speaker, which we should be looking at in this House of Commons which would assist people to move through this recessionary period, this worldwide recessionary period, with nowhere near the degree of harm which has occurred to date. Rather than simply considering the Income Tax Act in isolation, this particular piece of legislation should be put forward with a five-point program. First of all, we must have an industrial strategy. The impact of the Income Tax Act on shaping investment, shaping the redistribution of wealth in this country, and producing revenue for Government programs, is all for naught if there is not some idea of a plan, where we are going to go with that very fundamental instrument and how we are going to use it to shape the nature of industry in this country. It is an absolute waste of

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
time to put a statutory vehicle like the Income Tax Act before us without some kind of an economic plan.
The second point is that we need an employment strategy based on full employment. The Government over there is quite content to see the abysmal levels of unemployment continue in this country. A million and a half Canadians are unemployed, and that figure is certainly underestimated when we are talking about unemployment figures in most of the communities which I represent, whether it is Courtney, Campbell River, Northern Vancouver Island, Powell River, or the sunshine coast in British Columbia. Those communities are experiencing unemployment at rates of above 30 per cent, and that is a sort of official level. The figures do not count people on social assistance or people who have given up looking for work and do not qualify for UIC or Social Assistance. Therefore, what we should be doing today is talk about an employment strategy, a commitment on the part of this Parliament nationally to ensure that every Canadian has a right to employment, the right to a job.
The third point this Income Tax Act should be coupled with is an investment strategy. This is a major vehicle which can shape the nature of investment in this country, which can bring fulfilment to an industrial strategy and employment strategy. It is a waste of time to sit here this afternoon producing a lot of hot air in discussing an Income Tax Act which is not coupled with a logical economic plan. An investment strategy, without a broadly based industrial strategy will result in an insane investment of available capital. In my own Province of British Columbia today, the Premier of that Province is trying to explain to 1,900 men and women who have lost their jobs in the coal mines of southeastern British Columbia why this has come about. The reason it has come about, Mr. Speaker, is that the Province of British Columbia, and Ron Basford, a former Member of the Cabinet in this federal Government, have no concept of an appropriate investment scheme for that Province. Southeast coal has an over-capacity to provide coal to the Japanese. We have northeast coal; billions of dollars are being sunk into a project which will just increase the overcapacity in coal. Then, in my own riding we are going to dig another open-pit mine to undercut the price of both those projects and sell more coal to the Japanese in a shrinking, softening Japanese energy market. That is a waste of scarce and valuable capital. That is an absolutely insane resource development policy for this federal Government and the provincial Government to adopt. Where are your heads? Pull them out of the sand. Let us get this country together.
The fourth point we need a national co-operation program in this country. To sit here and talk about an Income Tax Act in isolation is ridiculous. We need a national co-operation program instead of the national conflict program which has been promoted by this Government. We have gone on long enough driving wedges between business, labour and Government for political ends. We must resolved the problems which are faced by so many Canadians in this recession. It is time to stop fighting and start cooperating and working together.
The six and five program was designed by the Liberals to pit business and Government against labour to create a fight, to envelop the population in a national internecine war. It is the most destructive thing which I have seen in my term in Parliament and what is a most destructive feature is the attitude, the failure to develop a program, and counting on short-term political gains by turning the population of Canada against organized labour, against the Public Service, and trying to entrap the business community into that obscene alliance. This Income Tax Act which we are debating this afternoon is a farce. What we need is a sense of direction. Japan, West Germany and other countries in the world have established a sense of direction. Where are we going? We need a re-commitment to social programs in this country. Health, education and welfare are the fundamental programs which underpin this country. There is an erosion of our health care system where the elderly, the poor, are going to suffer with user-pay programs. Students can no longer afford to attend our universities because costs are skyrocketing and their jobs are disappearing. Faculty members, who have spent years trying to stay on the leading edge with proper training, proper equipment, proper class sizes, in order to train the engineers and professionals of the future, are being driven out of the universities. We must make investments in those social programs.
These five points are absolutely important to establishing a direction, and we can sit here until hell freezes over, but at some point we are going to have to take positive action. At some point we are going to have to sit together and develop those five basic principles of national reconstruction. Until that happens, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people will continue to suffer.
There are two statutory vehicles which this Government could immediately put into place. One of them is the Income Tax Act. It is here before us this afternoon. Just recently we have looked at figures on the poverty level, Mr. Speaker, and we have found that 20 per cent of the people in this country take 80 per cent of the income. The other 20 per cent of the people at the bottom take about 10 per cent of the total income. That is a national obscenity. But it can be corrected and, with any sense of fair play, it has to be. It should be done by this legislation, but that question is being ignored. The Income Tax Act could also establish an investment program in this country which usefully uses our pools of capital to develop a diversified industrial strategy, in the forest industry, in the mines and in the shipbuilding industry, so that Canadians could have jobs. Those jobs are sitting there waiting and we are doing absolutely nothing. That is an absolute obscenity.
A second legislative vehicle is the combines law which could structure the state of competition, and the nature of business. Part of the problem we face today is the result of that enormous glut of greed which went on in this country with corporate takeovers. Instead of investing in this country in appropriate technology and manufacturing, bringing us to the leading competitive edge of the world's market, we watched our major corporations swallow up other corporations trying to make a
February 21, 1983

fast buck, cutting people out of work. We watched the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) spin his wheels, and the Government spin its wheels, by failing to bring forward an appropriate combines law which would structure the nature of our economy and would give small businesses a fair opportunity in the marketplace to compete with the large businesses, the Imperial Oils and the Royal Banks of this country.
With respect to the Bankruptcy Act, a third legislative vehicle we need in the short term to protect home owners and businessmen from the loss of their homes and business. The Income Tax Act is important, but if it stands alone, Mr. Speaker, we are spinning our wheels, we are producing nothing for Canadians. That Income Tax Act has to be coupled with a change in policy, and the five points which I outlined should be acted on now so we can make rational sense of this legislation before us today. Those five points should be coupled with at least three pieces of legislation which are already before this House, and certainly a program which would see a national employment strategy develop. Small businesses, Mr. Speaker, in many areas of this country have been hammered into the earth. We are looking at a situation today where the combined weight of Government, provincial and federal and municipal, are crushing them. We are talking about half of the small businesses in this country being driven into the ground by Government policy.

In entering into this debate on Bill C-139, we have been reminded that on December 7, 1982, the Government finally brought in the income tax legislation necessary to implement the November, 1981 budget some 13 months later. There were 389 days needed to bring Bill C-139 forward, which is a mammoth 297 page document. In spite of the fact that there have been what the Government calls extensive consultations, this document continues to be an attack on individual Canadians and on investment. It is the same attack that was announced in the November budget. The Government says that it is listening and makes a great deal about the fact that it is consulting. But it has become very clear that it is not responding. I enter this debate to reflect the views of Kitchener and Waterloo and southwestern Ontario, including parts of Woolwich Township and Elmira, the Township of Wellesley, New Hamburg and Wilmot Townships. It is an area of industry, farm and small business. I find that there is in this area a definite sense of repudiation of the direction taken in the Income Tax Act.
What is seen as being needed today is the incentive for the farmer, the small-business person and those in larger businesses in order that they may keep operating. What we see happening, rather, and the reason that this Bill is so inappropriate at this time, is a resort to survival tactics. Our small businesses are trying desperately to hold on. If the Government were interested in recovery and job creation, it would listen to what the small business are saying.
Income Tax
One has to ask why such changes should be introduced at this time in the face of what is happening. Some will ask where the incentives are. They certainly are not available to those in the Waterloo regional area who are part of our soaring statistics.
The Kitchener-Waterloo Record of February 4, 1983, entitles its lead story, "Recessions Victims". It states:
The unemployment rate in Waterloo region soared in January to the highest-ever recorded level-14.2 per cent-as 22,000 people were jobless out of an area work force of about 152,000, Statistics Canada said today.
That's up from 10.8 per cent unemployment in December, when an estimated 16,000 were jobless in an area work force of 151,000.
The article continues:
Locally, 15,402 people were registered in January at the Canada Employment Centre in Kitchener as unemployed and seeking work. At the end of December there were 14,157 registered.
This particular statistic is compounded by the fact that there is a lack of incentive in the tax system for our companies to continue. In the last few weeks, Leigh Instruments has announced that it intends to sell or close its Waterloo operation. At the same time, B. F. Goodrich is seeking to sell one of its divisions, the engineering products division. The combined potential loss of jobs in the next number of months may add another 800, plus the spin-off effects.
With the tax measures that we are asked to pass, come more penalties instead of incentives to create jobs in the workplace. As I look at Kitchener-Waterloo, and the Waterloo region which is home for a major part of Canada's insurance industry, I see that industry forced into a defensive position, especially in the life insurance capital dividend-accounts, as they affect estate planning.
I look at the farm community, and I see some of the finest farming area in southwestern Ontario. As a measure of the desperation that is a part of that community, and which shows the lack of faith it has in Government, we find the phenomenon of penny sales by the Farm Survival Association. On February 10, the Kitchener- Waterloo Record reported:
About 300 militant farmers shouted down the appointed auctioneer, persuaded him to step aside and proceeded to auction off an estimated $100,000 worth of farm machinery for $19.80 near here Wednesday.
After a $40,000 tractor sold for $2.20, a truck for $5.20 and a hay wagon for less than $1, the farmers ignored police warnings and cut through wire fences to make off with the machinery belonging to an area beef farmer.
The story went on to say that the low bidding, which is the latest tactic by the Association, was to aid strapped farmers who are unable to repay their bank loans.
What we have in the mood of the country at the moment is the danger of men and women pushed, in many cases to the limit, beginning to take the law into their own hands and the structure of our society beginning to break down. What we have in rural areas is not unfamiliar in the cities.
In recent weeks I have heard a number of comments about the style of operation of the officials of the Department of National Revenue. The question now is whether they are henchmen or whether they are public servants as they begin to try to feed a Government which is functionally bankrupt with

more revenue, which is like taking blood out of a stone. The time has come to begin building some structure of trust and incentive for those who have been working and want to continue to work.
Let me say another word in the time 1 have remaining about what this defensive posture is doing in the whole area of charities and what is being forced on our charities. The November, 1981 budget would have required charitable foundations to include the full amount of capital gains and losses in computing income, subject to the disbursement requirements.
In April, the original proposal was replaced with a requirement that foundations annually distribute an amount at least equal to 4.5 per cent of the fair market value of all their investment assets. Included was a formula to minimize the adverse impact of fluctuations in asset values, that is, disbursement in a single year will be based upon an average value of foundations' assets in the previous two fiscal years. A penalty will be imposed if the requirement is not disbursed in the given year.
Consultations with charitable foundations are continuing. The draft legislation is still outstanding. The new rules governing disbursement requirements will only apply in taxation years commencing after 1983. This will be the subject of legislation that will be introduced at a later date.
The whole matter of Bill C-139 and these income tax changes pertain not only to a lack of incentives to business, farms and industry, but also to charitable foundations and to charitable agencies themselves. I have already been espousing in the House the case of the need for a task force to review the give and take tax proposals which have been set forth by the national voluntary agencies. We are now set in the ridiculous context of Quebec-based charitable organizations being actually taken to court by National Revenue because they are pressing the Government to implement give and take tax reforms.
In all of these areas there is a need for incentives. Instead, we are faced in this House with a Bill that brings disincentive and disruption.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is an attack on Canadians, particularly those in the middle income sector. It has been introduced by a desperate Government-a Government without heart, a Government without conscience. The Government has reached the point that it needs to impose more taxes on Canadians primarily because, due to its own mismanagement, it does not have the wealth it needs in order to govern. Fairly or unfairly, Canadians must pay to maintain the burden of over-Government which is now in place.
The Government must be blamed for its lack of vision of what would happen in the OPEC situation. Like other nations, we are dependent on oil to pull us through this period. With Brazil, Venezuela and Mexico, we are over-dependent on the high price of OPEC oil and now, with the effect of the failing price of that oil on general revenues, the Government has had to revert to a heartless attack on the Canadian farmer, those
who set aside money for their retirement, on women and on the whole future of the country. This is an attack on those people by the Government which should be protecting them. It did not have the foresight to look beyond the income it was planning to receive through its most recent energy agreement. It believed it was going to receive millions of dollars because OPEC prices would rise to S60 per barrel. Now that the price has fallen, the Government is short of money.
This country should not be dependent on one industry. We are one of the most blessed nations in the world. Not only do we have oil, we also have one-third of the world's fresh water and mineral wealth not equalled by any other nation, a forestry capacity that would be the envy of many-we want nothing, Mr. Speaker. We have every resource, including the enormous talent of the men and women of the country.
If we had practised business principles as the Japanese and Germans did we would be the wealthiest nation in the world today. Just a decade ago this country ranked second amongst the leading nations of the world; today it ranks twentieth. That has happened because the Government is taking an increasingly large portion of the Gross National Product for its own expenses and is spending less and less on incentives for the private sector.
It is a generally accepted principle that the private sector creates wealth in society. It is the engine which creates growth in the economy. The public sector redistributes the wealth to make sure it is shared equitably.
Fifteen years ago it took 27 per cent of the Gross National Product to run Government, but today it takes 42 per cent. Let me show how dangerously close we are to a totally negative position, Mr. Speaker.
If the private sector is the engine for the creation of wealth, then any time a Government tries to distribute more wealth than it creates, say 50 per cent plus one penny, it is heading in a negative direction. Today, it takes 42 per cent of the total wealth of the country to run the Government. That is necessary because of the Government's mismanagement and ill-founded projections.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was in charge of energy he put an energy program in place. But he knew nothing about energy, Mr. Speaker. He believed that the OPEC price would keep going up, with no end. That was the whole basis of the arrangement. But OPEC collapsed and so did the Minister-so badly that they put him in charge of another Department.
That dependence on one industry in a country where many industries should flourish, has caused this desperate Government, without conscience, to attack the people in the middle income sector in their retirement years. It is taking away from them income that they earned throughout a lifetime. It is a desperate snatch at nickels and dimes. In the process they are taking away the incentive that would cause the country to grow.
We are coming dangerously close to the position of the Mexicos, the Venezuelas and the Brazils of the world. For
February 21, 1983

different reasons those countries are vulnerable because they depend on one industry. Mexico had some agricultural resource, a beef industry, some leather manufacturing and fruit production, but primarily its strength was based on petrodollars. That was even more the case with Venezuela. Brazil is an interesting contrast with Canada because it had a broader industrial base. But it made all its projections on the basis of petrodollars. Brazil is more heavily populated than Canada, and today it is on the verge of bankruptcy with a debt of $80 billion. With a population of only 24 million, this country has an accumulated debt of $140 billion.
The only reason that this country is sustained to some extent is that our forests are so large, our mineral wealth is so great, our fresh and salt water fisheries are so extensive. Otherwise, today we would be in the position of Mexico, Venezuela or Brazil.
It is because the Government believes that the price of oil would go up forever that this Bill, that attacks the farmers and retired people, is before us today. Before we pass legislation like this, the Government should do an enormous housecleaning.
Although the amount may be small in terms of total expenditures, we have to ask for the justification of the $800 per day for Donald Macdonald, the justification of the coal project connected with Alastair Gillespie who stands to make $750,000 on the basis of a $25,000 investment, for putting Michael Pitfield into the Senate or making sure that a former Minister of the Crown, Judd Buchanan, is able to establish a housing project in a national park in Banff. No other person could put such a construction unit in there because the area was not designated for that kind of housing. There are many other examples, Mr. Speaker.
Day after day the Government continues to waste money on inefficiencies and on large bureaucracies. There are Departments employing 2,000 people. We must ask why we need tax measures such as those before us if the Government cannot show that it is making every effort to restrain spending.
On the one hand we have no constraint being shown. There is no reason for the Liberals to believe that they need to hold back their spending, no reason for them not to pad the incomes of their friends, but they attack the retired people of the country, they attack farmers and small-businessmen! Small-business persons, according to this Bill, are greatly damaged by the fact that they cannot set aside moneys to invest for their future. In short, we have a Government which has caused an ill economy. It is treating it with an eyedropper. Somehow it believes that tremendous expenditures will bring about a recovery or that somehow its band-aid proposals or make-work programs are the answer. Painting the hall is not satisfactory for the creation of employment in the country. We need the private sector to be operating again for wealth to be generated in the country. Mr. Speaker, there is an old saying that an infinite number of monkeys using an infinite number of typewriters would eventually type all the great works. I think they completed their first one. It is called the Canadian Income Tax Act. Believe me, it keeps getting worse. The Bill we are discussing today, Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, does nothing to change this situation.
It will take more bananas.

That is right. We in Canada are subject to an income tax system which is based in the first instance on selfassessment. This means that it is up to us as individuals to determine how much income tax we owe and when and how it must be paid. It is not like sales tax where the rate is applied to a fixed amount, such as the price of goods, and included on an invoice, a cash register tape or a restaurant slip. Nor is income tax like property taxes, which local Governments calculate for us and on which they then send bills telling us how much we owe. No, when it comes to income tax, as I said, our system is such that the responsibility rests with us to determine how much we owe and when and how it must be paid.
Second, for decades it has been a well-established rule of jurisprudence that income tax laws be written in clear, unmistakable language. This is so because it is a self-assessing system. The most quoted statement by a court in this respect indicates:

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
It is not enough to attain a degree of precision which a person reading in good faith can understand, but it is necessary to attain, if possible, a degree of precision which a person reading in bad faith cannot misunderstand. It is all the better if he cannot pretend to misunderstand it.
Third, the cost of obtaining professional help in the preparation of a tax return for the vast majority of Canadians is not deductible for income tax purposes. To be able to deduct the cost of getting one's tax return prepared, one either has to have business income or a substantial volume of investment income. Thus, the very people who most need help-that is the wage earner or the taxpayer, with perhaps one T5 for interest or a bit of dividend income-cannot get a deduction.
All right, we have established the context. It is a fundamental principle of tax law that taxpayers should be able to understand the Act. Under Canadian law it is our responsibility to Figure out correctly how much tax we owe and when and how it is to be paid. For most Canadian taxpayers, the cost of getting help with their tax returns is not deductible for tax purposes. Yes, the Income Tax Act is an unmitigated mess. The reason I say this is that it is incomprehensible. Yet every taxpayer in the country is required by law to understand it; if we do not, the cost of obtaining help is probably not deductible; if we make mistakes on our returns, we may end up paying interest and penalties.
The entire Income Tax Act was revamped back in 1972. That is really not long ago, and that so-called reform of the Act was supposed to give us a well-thought-out, simpler tax system. Since 1972 there have been more than 30 major amending Acts. There were 350 changes in 1980-81 alone. Two months ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) introduced the latest amending Act. It contained 133 amendments, most of which are incomprehensible.
Like the Minister.

Yes, like the Minister. Bill C-139 is such a confusing document that neither I nor most other Hon. Members even know where to start in attempting to give it a fair appraisal.
It is not only desirable but absolutely imperative that taxpaying citizens of the country be able to communicate with their elected Government in terms that they both can understand. Is it unreasonable to expect that?
No.

No, not at all, yet here we have a massive contraption of some 295 pages which reflects no less than four budgets, near budgets, mini budgets, non-budgets and what have you. This does not count the number of minor statements, adjustments, changes, modifications and just plain retreats that this monstrosity reflects. In turn, it proposes amendments to a taxation system which nearly defied logical explanation at its inception. The inevitable result of all this is that the poor individual taxpayer is so totally helpless and at sea when confronted by a taxation problem that he cannot deal with it without professional help. I believe this is wrong in principle.
Bill C-139 is also harmful to insurance companies. There remains a clear disincentive for individuals to invest in life insurance, what has been until now the main investment vehicle for the less advantaged among the Canadian population. In other words, now people might just say, "What is the use of saving money, we might as well squander it, we won't worry about it, let the state take care of us when we reach age 65".
This disincentive takes two forms. First, policyholders are to be taxed on accrued income from their policies or deferred annuities. To tax a person on hypothetical income which he or she has not received is, in every case, to force a hardship on the investor. Investors must either scrimp and save from their current incomes to pay the tax or they must liquidate some of their investments to do so. In either case, there is created a strong disincentive to invest, and that is a likelihood that one more family and one more elderly couple will be dependent on the state when they reach the end of their working and earning lives.
There are many deficiencies in the new amendments to the Income Tax Act. Not only are there sections detrimental to the life insurance companies and to the people who hold policies, but businessmen who drive company cars are now being fingered for victimization at the hands of Revenue Canada. The Government is not taxing the folks in limousines. It is taxing the hard working, marathon-driving salesmen whom you find in Holiday Inns across the country in the late evening after a day spent selling their products. They are the people who keep this economy moving. We need these people. We are treating their company vehicles almost as a form of personal income and taking away what for many was one of the few tangible and enjoyable fringe benefits of their jobs.
The transition is very expensive, too.

What about the hardworking waitresses and waiters? Under the new terms of the Income Tax Act, they are being treated almost as common criminals. Their miserable incomes are being scrutinized with a magnifying glass.
A typical socialist ploy.
At the same time, the Government is going to pay Mr. Macdonald how much a day?
Eight hundred dollars a day.
Again, how much?
Eight hundred dollars a day.
Shame!
And $125 a day for expenses.

Mr. Macdonald is receiving $800 a day for activities of questionable benefit to the country. These waiters
February 21, 1983

and waitresses are honest people. They are hard working. They scrimp and save, and they serve you and me in restaurants across this great country. I am proud of them.
They are the salt of the earth.

1 submit that in carrying on this way against the little people of this nation, the Government is giving birth to unparalleled resentment, and it will be to their own detriment.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, my Party has no argument with the spirit of tax reform. We say, bring it on. However, only when that reform includes the closing of loopholes for the rich and influential and the simplifying of the tax return for the average citizen will the Government receive our full and uncompromising support.

Mr. Speaker, I must say I do not take a great deal of pleasure in speaking to this Bill this afternoon, particularly when it is a Bill designed to gouge the taxpayers of this nation of additional millions and millions of dollars. It seems a bit of a paradox this afternoon that we should be called upon as a Party to defend the rights of Canadians to be represented in this Parliament on the heels of a Bill that I now understand has been introduced by the Government to request an additional borrowing authority of $19 billion, which will be debated in due course.
It is a shameful Bill.

There is no question that this Bill will hit people who can ill afford to continue to support the wanton whims and ways of the Government that seems to be afflicted with some sort of desire to create a classless society. There will be no initiative left for anybody to take to work in a system that is responsible for the great country we have today. I am referring, of course, to the free enterprise system. This Government seems determined to wipe out all incentive for people to work and to contribute to society. It is a Government that seems determined to lead us down the path of socialism, a path
Income Tax
fraught with great danger and one that holds very little benefit for the people of Canada or any encouragement for them to support the continuance of the group opposite.
I want to talk about the burdens this Bill will impose on people, particularly the middle and low-income people of this country who will derive very little or no benefit from the lower taxes that it will create for them. The middle and low-income people will lose proportionately from partial deindexation. There is nothing left for these people in the country but a great amount of despair. This program is being implemented by a Government that is panicking in taking steps to gain revenue. The Bill introduced in the House which requires an additional $19 billion in borrowing authority is reflective of the sort of desperation which this Government is experiencing. This Government is penalizing those Canadians who continue to remain in the work force, either through diligence or through good fortune, to support their families.
We have dealt in the House before with the plight of life insurance holders. Those people are still being penalized. The language in Bill C-139 is so difficult as to be incomprehensible. It creates hardship to people. Those people who hold insurance policies and the companies that issue them are still terribly upset with the attitude of this Government and its absolute determination to penalize policy holders.
There is a particular class of people with whom I want to deal. They are the ones who are being hit hard. They include people of retirement age and people who have worked for years contributing to pension plans and now find themselves unable, because they are relatively few in number, to deal with the magnitude and the enormity of the burdens this Government is placing on them.
It is another attack on senior citizens.

It is a desperate state when the attack of the Government has to be directed primarily at low-income earners, middle-income earners and those who are least able to protect themselves, namely those people who are about to go on pension or have recently gone on pension.
This is a sad reflection on the direction the country is taking. I suspect that if Members on the other side of the House were truthful they would admit that their offices have been flooded in recent months, as has mine and those of most Members on this side of the House, by people Finding themselves in trouble with the income tax people and who have found it more difficult to deal with this bureaucracy over the years, and over the past months in particular. These people are receiving little or no satisfaction. It is the mentality of this Government and of the Department of National Revenue that in their eyes a person is guilty until that person is able to prove his or her innocence. That is completely contrary to the foundations or democracy laid down by our forefathers when this great country of ours, Canada, was set into motion some number of years ago.

Income Tax
I want to refer, as an example, to the sort of frustrations my constituents in Fundy-Royal are facing. They are basically hard working, conscientious people who, over the years, have developed, and substantially contributed to, the foundation of free enterprise and to the development of the country in no small way. Let me read a short paragraph from a piece of correspondence I received not too long ago which I think sums up very nicely the frustrations of these people. It states:
-my visions of a democracy have been greatly shattered and today I see just a hair's difference between a democracy and that of a totalitarian, socialistic Government. It appears that those individual rights of a citizen under the Charter of Rights is all a hoax and very hypocritical. It again appears that the time wasted for the constitution was merely a diversion from the real economic problems of the country with its energy and trading problems.
Your Honour will recall that at that time a good number of us who sat on this side of the House said just exactly that, that it was indeed a diversion from the economic problems. Now we know, months later, that a budget deficit which was initially forecast as being $9.8 billion was escalated to some $19 billion and went from there to $22 billion. If one checks the record, it will be found that we suggested the Minister of Finance at the time resign if it rose $3 billion over the $22 billion. Now we are told that it will be $27 billion.
Will it ever end?
Twenty-seven billion plus.

I am sorry, $27 billion plus. That is a sorry tale to be told. I suggest that the Government must take several proposals under advisement, one of them concerning educational benefits. The Government should release the students of this nation from that doctrine which seems to be "keep 'em down on the farm". It is deplorable that if one earns $40,000 a year and is attempting to send three children through college at $4,000 a year, by the time one ends up paying taxes, one probably ends up with an income of $8,000 with which to run the household and put food on the table. Of that $8,000, probably another $3,000 will be spent on federal and provincial sales taxes.
I will suggest to the Government that it place a moratorium on the Income Tax Act changes for a period of two years in order to build up some confidence in the business community of this nation, particularly the small business community that, as we all realize and understand, is the least able to defend itself but which provides the bulk of the job.
Let us put this country back on the road. Let us create an income tax system which can be defined in layman's terms so that even the tax people, the accountants who deal with tax reform, are able to understand it. That is not the case today.
I wish the people of this nation were fully aware of the fact that the frustrations we are experiencing have been caused solely at the hands of those people opposite who refuse to recognize the plight of the low and middle income people, the pensioners, those who are least able to defend themselves. I can
only say that unless there is a distinctive change in the attitudes of those who are directing the course of the nation, God help us.

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with Bill C-139, which is an Act to amend the statute law relating to Income Tax, I would like to point out something which was just brought to my attention today and which I feel is rather important. An article appearing in the Ottawa Citizen stated:
Businessmen who purchase gas by the gallon at a new anti-metric service station being opened Tuesday by a group of Conservative MPs can kiss their fuel tax rebates goodbye unless they convert their purchases to litres.
Anyone who uses a car for business is entitled to claim an excise tax rebate of 1.5 cents per litre-but apparently nothing per gallon.
"If you send us a rebate request in gallons, we'll just send it right back and ask you to correct it to litres", an official in the government's excise tax branch said Friday.
"It's illegal to sell gas by the gallon, so there's no way we are going to give rebates on anything but litres."
Consumers who buy their gas in gallons will have to convert their bills to litres to qualify for the rebates.
That is a lot of hogwash. Canada has been selling gasoline by the gallon in Provinces from British Columbia to Prince Edward Island since Canada became a nation. There is nothing illegal in Canada-yes, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I thank the Hon. Member for realizing that I am concerned. The issue, obviously, concerns the relevance. It is always an extremely difficult subject, particularly for the Chair, but perhaps the Hon. Member could relate his remarks to the subject matter of Bill C-139 from time to time. That would make it easier for the Chair.

For the benefit of the Speaker, Members of the Government and Hon. Members on this side of the House, I refer to Bill C-139 at page 65a which states, "This amendment would convert the measurement of area from imperial to metric."
Aha!

It states:
"-effective after 1981, the measurements referred to in the Act be converted into their metric equivalents."
With all due respect, my remarks are relevant to the Act. I am discussing the costs to the small businessman in the conversion of his land, his gas, his expenses in the running of his business, so that he can make a profit and pay some of that profit to the Government, so that he can continue on with his operations.
Since the Speaker has dealt with the isue of mandatory conversion to metric, I will draw to the attention of the House an invoice from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which I have in my hands, which became a tax item in the hands of the retailer who received the invoice. The retailer was Len Welch's Food Market Limited of 52 Hunter Street East, Peterborough, Ontario. The invoice was dated October
February 21, 1983

20, 1982 and stated that Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada wished to bill the dealer for a breakdown of fees involving one hour of inspection time and one and a half hours of travel time, for a total of two and a half hours at $20 per hour, amounting to $50, plus a distance of 78 miles at 22 cents per mile.
How many kilometres is that?

My question is, if it is not legal for a retail businessman to submit his expenses to the Government in imperial, that is, the price per gallon, why is it legal for the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which is responsible for the Metric Commission, to bill retail establishments across the country in so many cents per mile for so many gallons of gasoline?
Shame!

I draw the attention of Hon. Members opposite to the fact that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is responsible for the Metric Commission which has stated that it is mandatory to use metric measurements while it is invoicing businessmen in imperial measurements, right across the country. Why is Canada Post, which is also under the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, dispensing gasoline by the gallon at the main branch in Toronto, and why is the Armed Services base, under the Department of National Defence, dispensing its fuel to their required users in gallons? Why is Canada Post using imperial weigh scales to weigh parcels before they are shipped from post offices in Ontario.
I realize that I have only 10 minutes and I have only made one point, but 1 think I made it. I would like to deal with a few other points, and these are some of the reasons why we in the Opposition have been spending a considerable amount of time Fighting over one budget or another or one tax Bill or another since some three budgets ago.
I would like to put in my concluding remarks some of the things that we in Opposition have won on behalf of the people of Canada in our fight against unfair, prejudiced tax levies against the business community of this nation. I am going to list them.
First, the Government, because of the Opposition, will not tax employee health and dental benefits.
Second, the implementation of the shift in the manufacturers' sales tax to the wholesale level is delayed until 1984. It is only delayed, but it is delayed because we have consistently fought on that point of the necessity to reconsider that retrogressive measure.
Third, professionals such as doctors, dentists, lawyers, accountants and veterinarians, who are all eligible for the small business tax rate and those who would be ineligible if they were incorporated, will not be affected by the new tax treatment of work in process.
Income Tax
Fourth, the small business dividend distribution tax will only apply to dividends paid out of income earned in the taxation year, starting after the end of 1982, instead of being levied on dividends paid out after November 12, 1982.
Fifth, tax exemption for housing and travel benefits of employees in northern Canada will be extended one more year, and a modified system of taxing these benefits will be phased in over a four-year period, beginning January 1, 1984.
Sixth, the pre-budget rules on the tax treatment of capital gains in corporate re-organizations will continue to apply after the end of 1982. Any new proposals resulting from a current study by independent tax experts and subsequent consultations on a planned draft document will not apply to re-organizations that are substantially advanced from the date of the new proposal.
Seventh, the proposal to require that the interest on money borrowed to earn investment income only be deducted against investment income has been now withdrawn. However, interest on money borrowed to buy RRSP's or contribute to PDSP's or a pension plan may not be deducted as was proposed last November.
Eighth, there has been a reduction in the proposed automobile standby tax from 2.5 per cent to 2 per cent. The old rate was 1 per cent. That is one of the reasons we have been debating this for so long, it is not where it should be yet.
Ninth there are, modifications to the proposal relating to forward averaging for athletes and artists.
Finally, significant changes have been made to the November, 1981 proposal concerning periodic taxation of life insurance. Policies purchased before December 2, 1982, are not affected by Bill C-139.
I say to this House that there is no easy way to pass anything today brought in by a Government that has lost its credibility. It has shown its ineptness in balancing its own budget. Whether one is a businessman, a farmer, a homeowner, a housewife or whatever, if one cannot run the Government of Canada, one cannot run one's own home. The responsibilities of Members of Parliament are to live within the framework of the money that is available, at their disposal. If the Government cannot generate through its policies the necessary income, then it behooves this Government to show responsibility to curtail some of its budgeting expenses. One of those expenses that I am happy to announce has been cut down and on which this Government has finally seen the light, is that of the Metric Commission. They have told the Metric Commission of Canada that they have walked their last kilometer. Starting the end of this month, sectors in the Metric Commission will be phased out, and by the end of 1984 we will save an annual budget of $26 million by the abolition of the Metric Commission. Following the course of Mrs. Thatcher in Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States, we are now going to see the end of the Metric Commission in Canada. When we revert to voluntary in metric we will save the business community dollars, we will save this Government dollars and we will be more credible in the eyes of the people of this nation.
