speechtext: Before I recognize the next Hon. Member, it seems to me that the Chair owes at the very least a compliment to the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm). I have a vague feeling that I walked into a very well prepared process, but if I am vague about that I am very clear that the process was very well prepared and I admire it and I accept that the point of the Hon. Member was quite relevant.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with Bill C-139 from the perspective of a whole industry which was confused because of the tax structure in this country, an industry in which tremendous difficulty was created amongst fishermen and their families as a result of a confusing income tax law. This law caused untold difficulty in the fishing industry, particularly in the area of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island as well as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia.
The Bill we have today does nothing very much to clarify the situation for fishermen, but it does show a reversal of policies that were introduced in the November, 1981 budget. This action was taken by the Government in order, I think, to some extent to compensate for an audit of fishermen and the hardship that audit brought on, an audit which was done on both coasts, and went back many years over fishermen's income and which assessed fishermen a tremendous amount in income tax. A net of $30 million was assessed on an industry which was under some severe financial difficulties for a number of reasons: reduction in the quota, the amount available to fishermen; increases in the cost of energy and increases in the cost of interest to finance those industries. As a result, fishermen were faced with bills up to $500,000 in some cases but more often. 1 think, in the range of $1,200, $1,300, $1,500 and $2,000. That kind of income tax audit and the harassment from Revenue Canada in trying to collect brought hardship on families and concern from law-abiding citizens who were confused about the income tax laws, felt that they had filled in their income tax forms for a number of years well, they had received their payments from the Income Tax Department and had had no complaints for several years about how they were filling out their income tax forms. All of a sudden, during an audit, the income tax officials decided that these people had not been filling out their income tax properly, that their receipts were not adequate to qualify for the deductions they had made and, as a result, we had garnishees of up to 50 per cent of the income of those fishermen for the 1981 fishing season.
The answer to that and the answer to the number of representations from fishermen's groups about the audit and the way that the audit was being carried out was a proposed change in the Income Tax Act in the November, 1981 budget. Until then fishermen were able to pay two-thirds of their estimated income tax at the end of December and make up the difference at the end of the tax year. The Government felt that led the fishermen into some difficulties and suggested there should be a remission at source. Every time a fisherman sold fish to the processors, that income tax was to be paid.
The Government did not understand the sensitivity in the fishing industry, the requirement of fishermen to finance their operation during the fishing season. It did not understand that the fishermen had to use that source of income in the early part of the season to finance the purchase of gear, gasoline and meet other expenses.
Fortunately, fishermen were organized to some extent. There were petitions and letters from the Maritime Fishermens' Union of Prince Edward Island, the Fundy North Fishermen's Association, the United Maritime Fishermen's Co-op, the Eastern Federation of Fishermen, the Newfoundland Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union and the union in British Columbia. All made representations through the New Democratic Party and through petitions in the House objecting to the remission of income tax.
At one time the Minister of National Revenue was determined that it was the industry which proposed this change to the Income Tax Act. Their intervention was able to turn that around to the point where the Minister said that the remission of income tax at source could be voluntary. In the June, 1982 budget, it was indicated that that would be the provision in the Income Tax Act at that point. In the provision in this mass of documents before us, they no longer have the option of giving income tax at source. We are back to the status quo. What about the millions of Canadians who are not in the fortunate position of having a union or association to represent them? What about the millions who have to face the Income Tax Act on their own? They are faced with this cumbersome law which should have been reformed and simplified years ago. Instead, we are complicating it for these people.
There are accountants in my constituency who do not understand where we are going with the Income Tax Act, yet the fishermen, farmers and workers are expected to interpret this when working out their payable income tax. It is an impossibility. It just cannot be done.
Without the help of organizations, the average citizen is helpless to deal with this Government and the kind of legislation it imposes on Canadians. The sooner the Government realizes that income tax laws should benefit the citizen and not the lawyers, accountants and Government, the sooner we will have meaningful income tax reform. It should not be in a way which, as this Bill does, benefits the more wealthy in society. We should recognize the contribution of middle and low-income Canadians to the income of Government and the social programs which that income provides. Individual workers should be given credit for their work and they should receive some benefit from the Income Tax Act. They should at least have the opportunity to understand what they are supposed to be doing in terms of filing their income tax returns. Do not put them in the position in which fishermen were put in 1982 when they had to pay thousands of dollars in revenue to the Government after having believed they filed their income tax returns in a lawful manner.
February 21, 1983

This Bill is too complex for the average Canadian. As many Members of Parliament have said, it is too complex for them. Obviously it is too complex for those on the Government side.

Mr. Speaker, many of my colleagues on this side have already placed on the record the utter contempt of the Official Opposition toward Bill C-139. It is my intention during the next few minutes to highlight a couple of the points made by my colleagues, especially those who were Members of the Progressive Conservative task force on the budget that came down in November, 1981 and on which this Bill is largely based. I would also like to express a couple of my own thoughts and those of my constituents on this Bill.
At the outset, let me express my concern and a feeling bordering on disgust at the way this Liberal Government is proceeding with Bill C-139. In November 1981, the Government introduced one of the most complex, massive and comprehensive documents in income tax history. How complex is it? When my colleague, the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm), dealt specifically a few moments ago with metric, he was brought to order. Even such an intelligent occupant of the Chair as yourself, Mr. Speaker, did not know that in the amendments to the Income Tax Act there is a complete section which deals with metric conversion.
How complex is it? This was dealt with by the President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Ontario, J. Lyman Maclnnis. I understand this has been quoted during the debate by my colleagues. He gave an amusing and fascinating speech entitled "Cleaning Up Our Act (The Income Tax Act, That Is)". This senior partner of Touche, Ross and Company of Toronto had his audience on the floor when he got to an item which affects millions of taxpayers at all levels of incomeearning capacity and wealth, capital gains. I wish to quote him very briefly. Here is how he defined capital gains under the Income Tax Act:
There are three sections of the Act listed under the heading of "Capital Gains"
.. . Let's assume you are a logical person, so you start with the first section listed there. It is Section 39. When you find Section 39, you will also find that the fun is just beginning. Section 39 begins with a sentence that has 774 words, 28 commas and two semi-colons. Lincoln's entire Gettysburg address had only 267 words in it.
Section 39 has seven subsections. It refers you to ten other sections of the Act, which in turn refer you to another 40 sections. Section 39 also refers to a completely different law called "The Cultural Property Export and Import Act". And, I'll bet you all have a copy of that sitting on your coffee table!
So here we are. In trying to find out what a capital gain is we've already had to look at about 50 different sections of the Income Tax Act, and another completely different law. And, if you get that far, the reality then hits you that Section 39 only dealt with the word "Capital". To get a definition of the word "Gain' you have to look at Section 40. I'll spare us all that agony because Section 40 makes Section 39 look easy.
In my view it would be irresponsible and a disservice to Canadians to railroad Bill C-139 through all stages of debate. This complex Bill is far too long. Its implications go far too deeply for Canadians in all walks of life. It deserves full parliamentary scrutiny.
During the summer, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs examined a draft version of Bill
Income Tax
C-139. However, the draft Bill was incomplete and there had to be several changes. Even the Government admits the weakness of the Bill because of the number of changes it brought in insubsequent budgets and budgetary statements. Several of my colleagues have pointed out a couple of the serious weaknesses that the Government should be realizing and which this Parliament should be dealing with.
In the length of time, Mr. Speaker, that this Parliament has been called upon to deal with this huge Bill arising out of the November, 1981, budget, in human terms, over 500,000 people have lost their jobs and some 50,000 bankruptcies have been declared during this period. To put that into perspective, that means more than 500,000 jobs lost, a figure which is just about equal to the entire population of Hamilton, or Quebec City, or Calgary, or Winnipeg, or Edmonton. It is an incredible figure, Mr. Speaker, and it is something which indicates the deep concern Canadians have about the way the Government is running the country, and the very real concern which we in this Party have heard expressed by millions of Canadians as we travel across the country, and by letters coming into all of our offices.
This concern indicates that this approach to tax reform is wrong. It is dead wrong. Bill C-139 is hitting the lower and middle class income groups in so many different ways that it is going to take Canadians a long time to realize just how serious the impact will be as a result of this Bill.
The hardest hit, of course, will be the lower and middle income Canadians who will gain little or nothing from the lowering of marginal tax rates and who will lose proportionately more from partial de-indexation. The increased taxation of employee benefits will hit hardest at those in the lower and middle income brackets. It will encourage employees to seek higher wage settlements at a time when moderation is required. The taxation of housing loans will make it harder to recruit employees who must relocate. For those who already have loans, the taxation of this benefit may represent a rude shock which was not anticipated when an employee accepted a housing loan as part of his relocation package.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), pointed out, the retirement nestegg is created by paying off the family farm. This is why farmers in my riding, farmers all over the country, but particularly the small farmers who I am familiar with in southern and southwestern Ontario, are hit very hard by Bill C-139. The Liberal Party and its bureaucrats simply do not understand that the family farm is the Canadian farmer's pension plan.
All of our constituents work hard on a day-to-day basis to put something aside for retirement. And as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Simcoe North has reported during this debate, that retirement nestegg is created by paying off the family farm. What the farmer does is sell the farm and take back a mortgage. Before the Government changed the rules, a farmer could sell his farm and invest the capital gain portion in

February 21, 1983
Income Tax
an income averaging annuity. That allowed him to plan for retirement. He could calculate his chances for surviving, and for how long, and invest the money and get an annuity. The Liberals have changed all that, and they do not care. They do not have any idea of what is happening out there. They have no idea whatsoever what is happening, particularly to farmers in Canada who now face an even greater uncertainty if the provisions of Bill C-139 go through.
The Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) touched on much the same plight which is hitting the farmers. He put on record how the income tax legislation relates to the farmers in Manitoba, and the same applies to farmers in Hamilton-Wentworth. Every Hon. Member who represents a rural riding has been noting the number of people who come to our offices to complain about the tax system and the manner in which the tax Department is treating individual taxpayers. There is an increasing number of representations being made to our offices, Mr. Speaker, about what constitutes a hobby farm and how the income tax Department is going to be able to treat those people who own hobby farms equitably. This legislation does not speak to this at all, Mr. Speaker.
Finally, I would like to read into the record one letter which came from a constituent in Hannon, in my area:
Dear Sir,
I am writing to you about the college tuition fee income tax deduction, as of now only the student can claim this deduction. Now it seems to me that if the student has no income whatsoever, as in my son's case, as he cannot get a job, this means that the parents are paying the tuition fees, so why can't the head of the household claim these fees as a deduction.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say that there are many millions of Canadians out there whose individual situations will be drastically affected by Bill C-139, if it goes through as the Government is now proposing to ram it through. We, on this side, find that approach unacceptable and we are going to bat for those millions of Canadians who are concerned about what is happening to them in an income tax sense with unfair taxation, even if the Government side will not.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today I was addressing a large gathering of secretaries and administrative assistants from across the country. During the course of my remarks, I happened to mentioned that I would be returning to Ottawa to take part in the debate on the amendments to the Income Tax Act later today. I can tell you, sir, that a groan went up from that audience, not because I said I was going to go back to Ottawa to take part in this debate, but because the very mention of the Income Tax Act, and further amendments to it, brought a groan from them, as it is bringing a groan from Canadians from one coast to the other.
What those women said to me when I mentioned this, sir, was, "Is there anybody in Ottawa who can write anything at all about the income tax in straightforward, direct terms which we can understand?" They told me that what the Government is sending to them is totally incomprehensible. And these are women who work in offices, who transact business, who do
detailed studies of various financial matter every day. But what they are receiving, and what their offices are receiving, with regard to income tax is totally incomprehensible to them.
It is increasingly incomprehensible, not only to Hon. Members of Parliament, but to the general public, just how the Government House Leader (Mr. Pinard) is ordering the business of this House. I would say to him that this tax Bill, this huge Bill we now have before us, is the best example I know of, of the Government's incomprehensible and, indeed, I would say, inscrutable way of processing legislation through this House. What we have is a document 300 pages long with 134 different tax changes. That is almost impossible to digest, whether you happen to try it mentally or physically. Many of the measures contained in it need detailed study and analysis just to see what their impact is going to be on average Canadians. This is a big document, it is a hefty document, and I sometimes wonder if the Government is not trying to calculate the worth of this document by its weight.
Quite seriously, this Bill emerges from what I would consider the incomprehensible Fiscal policy of this Government stretching back over many months, indeed, years. We had that well-remembered budget in November, 1981. No Canadian will forget that budget the former Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brought down. No one will ever forget the way it was put forward, the way it was countermanded, changed, corrected, and parts withdrawn. The only tragedy is that it was not all withdrawn.
Before the measures in that particular budget were passed through the House, another budget was introduced, in June of last year. That budget contained even more complex measures. In October of last year we saw an economic statement which also introduced new measures. Just the other day, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) came before the Flouse with his latest projections, saying he wanted authority from the House to borrow an additional $19 billion. That is not $19 million, something which we might have found comprehensible, but an additional $19 billion. Of course, none of the projections he gave us for the deficit, unemployment or inflation had any relation to the economic statement of October, 1982 or the November or June budgets. In each case, the projections for the deficit have escalated. The projections continue to soar with every passing month.
What is worse, the financial picture of Canada is in a total state of confusion. Is it any wonder, given that confusion and financial mess, that the Government wants to push this Bill through with the least possible scrutiny? That is what is happening right now. The Government is telling the House and the general public that it wants to get this Bill through, regardless of the fact that the impact of many of its changes will be detrimental to individual Canadians, small businesses and corporations. Indeed, the Government is using a not so subtle form of blackmail to make sure they bring down the hammer of their majority on this Bill. It is trying to insinuate that, without the passage of this Bill, tax refunds cannot be
February 21, 1983

sent out to the many millions of Canadians who will be receiving them. That is downright duplicity on the part of this Government. No one knows better than that crowd over there that computers of Revenue Canada will be down from the middle of February to the end of March for reprogramming. There can be no tax refunds sent out during that period of time and they will not be available until April or even May of this year. As the Minister knows, some of the officials in Revenue Canada have had the honesty to admit that fact. However, none of the Government Ministers have deigned to do so.
The scrutiny of the 134 tax changes in this Bill will not hold up the mailing out of tax refunds. What will hold up the mailing out of those tax refunds is the Government's lack of planning in the manner in which the Department handles tax refunds.
When we get into the Committee of the Whole, we will have an opportunity to question the Minister on some of the more repugnant measures contained in this Bill. I want to mention a few of them in the time I have left. They are measures such as the taxation of employee benefits, the replacement of general averaging and income averaging annuity contracts by forward averaging, and the imposition of the 12.5 per cent small business redistribution tax. I want to say something about those particular measures.
Before I do so, I want to mention an issue that has been raised by Members on both sides of the House concerning individual tax reforms which have been sent out to Canadians all across the country. 1 was simply appalled to see confidential and private information printed on those forms; marital status, last year's income and social insurance numbers of individuals, with no security that these forms will actually land in the hands of the individuals to whom they are directed. There is no security or guarantee whatsoever. In fact, the release of that material on the 1982 Income Tax returns is surely a contravention of the Protection of Privacy Act. These Acts were put through by the House, yet the Government turns around and refutes them.
I have had dozens of people call my office about this particular issue. I have had many complaints from people who are concerned about what is happening here. These people are very upset that this private and confidential information which pertains to them particularly is now being made available for others to use. What they are most worried about is that if this particular step is currently being taken by the Government, what will it do next? What other information will it make available to the general public? Surely, if the Government makes that type of information available on the Income Tax forms it is sending out this year, it should make a definite determination right now that next year's returns will not contain the same private and confidential information.

Mr. Speaker, it seems the excellent speech by the Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has the Minister worked up. It will be difficult to get the Minister more excited than he now is
Adjournment Debate
in the time I have left. The points made by the Hon. Member were excellent. Perhaps that is why the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) is excited.
My colleague spoke about this legislation being incomprehensible. People in my riding are telling me about their frustration and bewilderment over the complex Income Tax Act that has evolved over the last 20 years. Because people feel the Income Tax Act is unfair they try to find ways around it or they feel they must hire accountants at tremendous cost to keep them within the law. Billions of dollars of tax revenue are being lost each year as people try to get around the Act.
It is not very difficult to get around the Act with so many changes to it, such as the 139 additions from the last few budgets. We have had budget after budget with clause after clause added to the Income Tax Act. As a result, people revert to such procedures as the barter and cash systems, with jobs performed on a cash basis or in return for another project. Canadians are resorting to this practice because they feel too much money is being taken from them by the Government. Therefore, the underground movement begins. We, as parliamentarians, do not want that. As legislators, we do not want to enact legislation that people feel is unfair. However, that is the situation with this Bill.
The Minister who introduced these budgets said that we must close the loopholes. These loopholes exist in a tax system under which people have set up their businesses on which they depend for the income to raise their families. They are now called loopholes by the Government. Of course, as it discovers the political problems resulting from its budgets the Government backs off. In turn, the people and businesses of this nation sit back and wonder when the Government will stop its vacillation. The Government must determine the investment it should be making in the future, and how taxes should be levied in the future as well.
I have mentioned some of the difficulties this system of taxation is causing Canadians, Mr. Speaker. There are many other things I wish to say, but perhaps I may do that on another day, and call it six o'clock now.

INDUSTRIAL SAFETY AND HEALTH-DUST HAZARD IN GRAIN ELEVATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Member with a particular interest in occupational health and safety,

February 21, 1983
Adjournment Debate
I have followed the disappointingly slow progress of negotiations with grain elevator operators over a number of years. Grain dust within elevators has long been considered a cause of serious lung disease. Furthermore, because the dust is combustible, high levels often constitute a fire and explosion hazard.
In 1972 the Government and the industry agreed on a system of voluntary compliance to improve the protection of workers. When that failed to produce results, the Department of Labour established a schedule with a three-year deadline, which in turn had to be extended by a further 18 months. However, by the end of 1982, 32 per cent of the 53 large terminal and transfer elevators, and 31 per cent of the 2,900 smaller primary elevators, were still without safe dust control measures. Clearly, persuasion has not worked and the time has come to enforce standards to protect the health of Canadian workers in grain elevators. I regret very much that we have not been able to arrive at voluntary compliance. This has always been the Canadian way. Voluntary standards are surely preferable in an industry. Management and workers surely have the same interest in maintaining a safe and healthy workplace. Where management has set up health and safety committees in other industries, the results have usually gone far beyond the immediate health and safety aspects, and have tended to result in better management-worker relations and higher productivity. There have been a lot of other gains.
It is unfortunate that in this particular industry progress has been slow, for whatever reason. I can understand that one reason may be the uncertainty about future rail planning and the high cost of installing safety measures. When human health and lives are at stake, surely that must be the overriding factor. The evidence is in that people who have worked in the grain industry are showing very definite signs of lung damage. As well, in 1978 there was a series of bad accidents in American terminals and we would not want to see that happen here.
In a recent speech the Minister said that he would have preferred to see voluntary standards work. He said that selfregulation is not predicated on a compromise in objectives-in this case the health and safety of the employee-but rather, it is predicated on a shared objective of management and labour and an agreed means of achieving it.
In 1978 this House passed amendments to the Canada Labour Code which gave workers the right to refuse to work if they thought conditions were unsafe and if other measures had failed to bring about the correction of difficulties. The refusal to work is a very serious decision for workers to arrive at. The voluntary improvement of conditions using the vehicle of health and safety committees with workers and management both involved is surely a much better decision. In these times particularly, when we talk about productivity, many of us are very much aware that we lose far more days of work through illness, industrial accident and injury than we do through strikes.
The issue of workers' safety is one which goes far beyond the grain industry. It needs to be addressed in every facet of Canadian working life. I had hoped that at this particular time, when, because of the six and five program bargaining on monetary issues is limited, we might have seen some very creative bargaining with good faith on both sides on occupational health and safety issues.

speechtext:

It should be noted that when the Minster of Labour (Mr. Caccia) replied to her question last week he was very concerned about the entire occupational safety and health of workers in the grain industry. In fact, industry officials have been informed that they will be required to show Labour Canada why they have not complied with the regulatory requirements for occupational safety and health. This directive places the onus on various companies to come up with some rationale or reason why they have not complied. I assure the Hon. Member that the Department of Labour will be following up on this matter very closely.
The primary objective of Labour Canada's grain dust program was to protect the pulmonary health of grain workers by reducing the amount of airborne dust in elevators. Included also was a requirement for environmental and medical surveillance. The directive contained specific objectives to be accomplished within certain time frames in accordance with established criteria. I wish to underline that certain objectives must now be met within a specified time frame. The industry will be contacted in the very near future and advised of the details of Labour Canada's follow-up plans, so that there can be no misunderstanding by the Department of Labour or the industry as a whole. I assure the Hon. Member that this matter is receiving the utmost attention of Labour Canada, the Minister and all his officials.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: ENERGY-NEGOTIATIONS BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND NEWFOUNDLAND ON OFFSHORE RESOURCES. (B) TELEXED MESSAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with a question which I asked on January 26 of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) that dealt with negotiations between the federal Government and Newfoundland on offshore resources.
Since asking that question, the Newfoundland Supreme Court on appeal brought down a decision, last Thursday, I think it was, in which it found that the Province of Newfoundland does not have legal ownership of the oil and gas and other minerals which lie off the shores of Newfoundland and Labrador. It has found, for technical, legal reasons, reasons of precedents and obscure points of law, which of course are dealt
February 21, 1983

with in these kinds of court cases, that technically and legally the Government of Canada owns these resources. That judgment will be appealed, of course, to the Supreme Court of Canada. There is another case starting tomorrow in the Supreme Court of Canada involving the very same issues on a reference by the Government of Canada.
First 1 want to say that I have the highest respect and regard for the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland, as I have for the Supreme Court of Canada. I want now to turn to the parliamentary assistant and make the point that it matters not a whit what is the legal position. It does not matter whether or not the Government of Canada is found to be the legal owner of these resources. In equity and justice, they were all brought into Canada as resources by Newfoundland when Newfoundland joined Canada on March 31, 1949; two-thirds of the whole East Coast of Canada was brought into Confederation by Newfoundland. That is all of the area off Newfoundland, the Continental Shelf and off Labrador. Two-thirds of the whole Canadian East Coast offshore was brought into Confederation by Newfoundland. If Newfoundland had not joined Confederation, those resources would not have belonged to Canada at all.
We had a comparable situation in Canada in the period before 1930. I draw this to the Minister's attention. Up until 1930 neither Saskatchewan, Alberta nor Manitoba owned their mineral or natural resources under the soil of those three provinces. Those provinces were created from lands which the Dominion of Canada acquired, the lands of Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1905 and the lands of Manitoba, of course, earlier.
The legislation and the law was quite clear. The Government of Canada retained ownership of all the resources in those three western provinces. In 1930, because it was felt to be just and equitable under our system of confederation-the Canadian Constitution-to take such action, the Government of Canada and this House enacted legislation to provide for a transfer of ownership of those mineral resources from the Dominion of Canada to those three provinces; Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Had that not been done, Alberta and Saskatchewan and their Governments would not today be in the healthy financial situation they are now in. Action was taken, and I will quote from the debates at the time. In this particular case the debate is dealing with Manitoba. The debate reads that the Government should place Manitoba:
-in a position of equality with the other provinces of Confederation with respect to the administration and control of its natural resources as from its entrance into Confederation in 1870.
What the Government must do to put Newfoundland and Labrador , Nova Scotia and other maritime provinces in a position of equality with the other provinces of Confederation, is to have this House pass legislation, and, if necessary pass the necessary amendments to the Constitution to provide for ownership of these offshore resources in the provinces off whose shores they lie. That is the only just and equitable position that can be taken by any Government that cares in this country. Those provinces are, by the way, the have-not provinces. Then they can be given an equal chance with the
Adjournment Debate
other, let's call them, land-locked provinces in Canada who do now own their resources.
I point out that when the boundaries of Ontario and Quebec were enlarged at the beginning of this century, by including in their areas large portions of what is now the Northwest Territories and the Arctic regions, the resources were also transferred to those provinces. If Newfoundland in this particular case is to have an equal position in Confederation with the other provinces, the action taken in 1930 has to be taken again. It was later on July 15, 1930 for Manitoba and on October 1, 1930 for Alberta and Saskatchewan.
The position of our national Party, and my position, as exemplified in a letter written to all the Provinces of Canada on September 12 or 14 of 1979, when we were in office by the then Prime Minister, Mr. Clark, is that we were carrying out that exact policy. That is our policy, and it will be our policy when we resume office again. We will transfer ownership to the offshore provinces of all the offshore oil and gas and other mineral resources. The "offshore" provinces will be put in the exact same situation as the other provinces of Canada. They will then be able to make their own way, stand on their own feet economically and have control over activity that is going to be impinging most heavily on them, no matter who has legal ownership of the particular resources. That is the only fair and equitable thing to do.
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary today-I suppose he cannot give me the answer-to plead with his Minister and the Government to cease their attempts to bully and browbeat the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and to change its policy, and announce in the next several weeks that the Government will transfer and convey to Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, P.E.I., and British Columbia rights of ownership, management and control over those resources. Therefore, the principles of Confederation will apply equally to all provinces including the less well endowed ones.
I want to appeal to the Government, Mr. Speaker. It could get the Hibernia development under way. It could start introducing the opportunity for some prosperity in eastern Canada if it moved now to carry out my advice. Wait no longer. If you, the Government, do not do that, I for one will support the Government of Newfoundland in its position that never should it agree to anything less. When we have a chance to form the administration in this country we will see that these things are carried out.

FISHERIES-KIRBY TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS- PRESENTATION OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT SECURE EQUITY IN EAST COAST FISH PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss the question of Thursday, February 17, following the release of the Kirby Report on the Atlantic fishing industry. I would like to remind the Parliamentary Secretary that in the beginning the Kirby Task Force was formed to look into the severe financial difficulty in which the fishing industry found itself, particularly in Newfoundland, but also in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Labrador.
In November of 1981, ten fish plants shut down in Atlantic Canada. In January of 1982 The Globe and Mail reported:
National Sea . . . owes the Bank of Nova Scotia $100 million and the government of Nova Scotia ... $10 million. The Lake Group avoided bankruptcy through an 11th hour infusion of federal and provincial funds that will allow it to reopen its plants at Grand Bank and Galtois. They had been closed since late summer."
The Financial Post reported:
Fishery Products Ltd. last week announced its plant at St. Anthony ... had lost $10 million in the past four years and might not open at all this year.
On August 13, 1981, St. John's Evening Telegram reported:
Last Tuesday ... National Sea Products Ltd. announced it was shutting down its plant in St. John's and others in Nova Scotia, indefinitely ... laying off some 1800 workers-
The Kirby Report was initially supposed to be tabled, or at least given to the Government, in the summer of 1982. After a long one-year wait the report was made public, yet the Minister is hesitant about tabling it in the House of Commons so that the Forestries and Fisheries Committee can deal with it in any meaningful way. That report did not address the urgent problem of the fishing industry. In fact, Mr. Kirby and the Minister announced that it would be another two months before we would know about the financial conditions and the restructuring of the fishing industry. I do not think it is adequate that a report which has cost the Canadian taxpayer some two million dollars should not deal with the uncertainty of many communities in the Atlantic fisheries, including the still unemployed people in Ingall's Head, New Brunswick and Georgetown, Prince Edward Island. When I was there this weekend, I was questioned about the Georgetown, P.E.I., plant, whether it would be opening or not. I had to admit that 1
February 21, 1983

did not know, that we had to wait two more months before the Government's restructuring program would be announced. We also have uncertainty in Lewisporte, Bridgeport and Jackson's Arm, Newfoundland, and Lismore, Nova Scotia, and the people of Grand Banks and Burin are fighting desperately to save their plants and the income of plantworkers in those communities.
The Report of the Task Force that started out as a result of thousands and thousands of plantworkers being unemployed in Atlantic Canada still has not addressed that problem. I think that is unfortunate because people are dependent on the fishing industry, and they have not really been dealt with in a fair way to this point by the Government.
There is some suggestion in Mr. Kirby's comments that some of those plants will never open again. There is some suggestion in the report that in order to open we may have to depend on some foreign capital. Some of his recommendations and options call for the possibility of the Atlantic fisheries, including the possibility of Fishery Products, Lakes Group and Nickerson, coming under a Crown corporation. We have no certainty that that is going to occur.
We now know how desperate the situation is. Kirby estimates, as a result of very detailed accounting investigations, that there is some $520 million of debt in the Atlantic fisheries, and there will have to be a massive amount of money put into that industry to protect this fleet and the jobs of fishermen. The Minister was not able to say whether or not there would be any equity position of Canadian taxpayers, or any say on the Board of Directors by community and plantworkers and fishermen if we are again going to bail out the fishing industry, as we did in 1974 with a $200 million bail-out, only to have companies that were no longer viable at that time come back to the Canadian taxpayer in 1982 and 1983 for another major infusion of capital.
It is not good enough to carry on with the same management scheme, and not good enough to say that this report will bring greater benefits to fishermen in 1985. The report does not deal with a better price for fishermen. It says that fishermen will have to carry out mandatory bleeding and gutting on their vessels to deliver a better product to the dock. However, it does not say that that better product will demand a better price. It says that a processor should be able to give a better price, but there is no mandatory provision whereby processors must guarantee fishermen a better price.
We are disappointed in the report because it does not deal with the key issue. We are disappointed that we cannot tell people in Georgetown, Fermeuse, Trepassey, Burin and Grand Bank that they are indeed going to have a fish plant with employment for their community. This Government has a responsibility to see that those jobs are protected and to ensure, when Canadian taxpayers' money goes into a bail-out,
Adjournment Debate
that there is some equity for the amount of money, and that the processors will be involved in the decision making.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: FISHERIES-KIRBY TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS- PRESENTATION OF GOVERNMENT RESPONSE. (B) REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT SECURE EQUITY IN EAST COAST FISH PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in releasing the report of the task force on Atlantic Fisheries on February 17, 1983, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) made clear that the task force had two mandates. The first mandate was to advise the Government on the long-term policies it should implement to promote a healthy fishery in the future. It is that mandate which has been fulfilled with the release of the task force report.
The second mandate of the task force was to advise the Government on how to deal with the specific requests which came in late 1981 for financial assistance from the Lake Group and H. B. Nickerson and Sons Limited, both important integrated offshore groundfish companies.
As the Minister stated, it quickly became clear that what was required to solve the immediate financial crisis of these companies was substantial restructuring of the offshore processing sector. Such restructuring is more complicated than simply handing out financial assistance. The whole process became much more complicated when, in November of 1982, Fishery Products Limited also came forward with a request for financial assistance. The problem of how to put the activities of these three companies on a viable footing is extremely complex and can only be worked out through a process of negotiations with all interested parties, including the major creditors, provincial Governments and, of course, the Government of Canada. These negotiations are now in their final stages. They are critical both for industry and the Atlantic region.
The companies concerned have plants in many communities throughout the region. These plants are, in many cases, the lifeblood of the communities in which they are located. The Government is very much aware of the sentiments expressed by the Hon. Member and we hope we can make those decisions in addressing these problems very soon.
These negotiations, which have been going on for some months, are currently in a very delicate stage, and I am not in a position to go into any detail at the present time. I can say, however, that the objective of these negotiations is not to bail out existing shareholders. Rather, it is to restore the offshore sector to reasonable financial health so that it can continue to generate the jobs upon which so many communities and individuals depend. The extent to which the Government might have to become involved to achieve this objective, and the form in which such involvement might take, will be a matter for negotiation.
